title: Causal AI: Evaluating AI Workflows on HPC Environments Using Causal Testing
abstract:
As AI and machine learning become central to scientific research, the ability to rigorously verify their behaviour has struggled to keep up. Traditional software testing breaks down in this context: scientific pipelines rarely have a single correct output to test against, their configuration spaces are vast, and their stochastic nature makes it difficult to distinguish genuine errors from expected variation. The consequence is that many scientific AI systems are deployed with limited understanding of what actually drives their outputs.
Causal testing offers a principled alternative. By encoding domain knowledge as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) - a structured representation of the cause-and-effect relationships between variables, such as batch size or floating point precision - researchers can formally test whether their pipeline behaves as expected, using data already collected from prior runs. This removes the need for expensive re-experimentation and makes verification tractable even at HPC scale.
This poster presents causal-ai, an open-source tool developed as part of the N8 CIR AI4Science project to improve the ability of evaluating complex AI/ML workflows on HPC systems. The tool provides direct HPC integration, a command-line interface, and worked case studies across image classification and video domain adaptation pipelines. Cross-cluster comparisons further reveal platform-dependent effects that conventional evaluation metrics do not capture.

title: Kill your shell scripts: Reproducible workflow management with Snakemake
abstract:
You have a process to automate. It only has a couple of steps, one after the other, so you write a shell script. Then, you add more steps. Perhaps you want to cache some of the intermediary state, and only re-run when the underlying data change, to save time. And maybe what final stage you run depends on what output you’re looking for. Before long, you’re either writing a rat’s nest of ad-hoc code looking after these edge cases, or writing your own domain-specific language within Bash to handle this task of… Workflow Management.
It turns out that you are far from the first person to have encountered the problem of workflow management, and there are many mature tools available to reduce your maintenance burden and let you focus on your specific workflows of interest. In this walkthrough I’ll introduce how to use Snakemake, a workflow manager developed in life science and commonly used in particle physics, but applicable for many purposes more widely. Topics I’ll cover include how to define rules that depend on the output of other rules, templated rules that can work for a variety of input files, and rules depending on some external metadata or configuration; how to parallelise running a workflow on a single machine; and how to run steps of a workflow using external computing resources such as an HPC cluster.

title: Coding Confessions: Normalising Failure in Research Software
abstract:
What?
At Coding Confessions RSEs talk openly about mistakes they've made developing software, running systems or managing projects. First developed during the SSI’s Collaborations Workshop Hackday 2021, Coding Confessions panels took place at RSECon 2021, 2022 and 2023. This year we are broadening the scope to provide a wider discussion and cover some of the commonly recurring themes including imposter syndrome, visibility of hidden roles, AI going wrong and management of junior staff.
Why?
Mental health is an important issue for RSEs (34% of RSEs have experienced a mental health condition since becoming RSEs - 2022 RSE Mental Health Survey). RSEs should work in environments where they can freely discuss their mistakes, yet often lack confidence when publishing or submitting their code for review or asking for help navigating other challenges. Common reasons for this include my code “isn’t good enough or isn’t complete enough”, alongside wider professional anxieties such as “I should know this”, “I can’t ask for help”, or “I don’t belong here”. We encourage people to share their insecurities to normalise talking about mistakes and knowledge gaps.
How?
“Traditional” Coding Confessions events (as run 2021-2023) consisted of a panel where several RSEs talked about mistakes they've made in software they've developed. This year we will be expanding to a broader discussion. We will begin with a traditional coding confessions panel followed by some short talks and a group discussion. We will publish blog posts with OLS, SSI or ConveRSE to disseminate the findings of this session.

title: Where does the rigor go? Research software and the future of trustworthy science.
abstract: Generative AI now makes it dramatically easier to produce something that looks like research: analysis code, figures, literature reviews, even whole papers. The mechanisms research relies on to establish trust were built for a slower, human-paced enterprise, and they are struggling with the volume. Software got here first: this community has a two-year head start on questions the rest of research is only beginning to ask, and RSE work is already changing shape, away from writing code for researchers and toward specification, verification, and the judgment that makes AI-assisted work trustworthy. I'll share observations from my perspectives as a funder, a journal editor, and a long-time member of this community and offer some thoughts on where research software engineering goes next.

title: Green RSE Special Interest Group: Building a Environmental Skills and Knowledge in the RSE Community.
abstract:
There is an urgent need to reduce the environmental impact of research computing. While many research institutions have high-level commitments to emissions reductions, it is not always clear how these will be achieved. The UKRI DRI Net Zero scoping report found that in many cases this transition is hindered not by a lack of knowledge, but by insufficient knowledge-sharing and structures to enable behaviour change.
RSEs are well placed to help drive this transition - both through their technical skills and by acting as agents of knowledge exchange across research communities. Despite this, environmental sustainability is seldom an official part of the RSE roles.
The Green RSE Special Interest Group (https://socrse.github.io/green-sig/) is working to change this by building a supportive community that helps RSEs play an active role in the transition to sustainable research computing. In this submission, we reflect on two years of progress, including: defining what environmental sustainability means within the RSE role; identifying best practices for environmentally responsible software; and developing resources to improve code efficiency and reduce energy usage.
Looking ahead, we argue that realising the potential of RSEs as sustainability champions will require formal recognition of green skills within RSE career frameworks, dedicated training pathways, and stronger institutional mandates that make sustainability a core part of RSE roles. The Green RSE SIG is committed to building the community and resources to make this possible.

title: Using Causal Reasoning to Test Scientific Software
abstract:
From predicting the weather to simulating disease transmission, scientific software plays an increasingly pivotal role in developing scientific understanding that informs our everyday lives. However, they are also some of the most difficult software systems to properly test. Because the developers are often the scientists themselves, they may not be familiar with established testing techniques and are likely to focus on scientific results rather than software quality. From a technical standpoint, scientific software systems tend to exhibit several characteristics that make traditional testing techniques impractical and often insufficient. They have large, complex input spaces, are computationally expensive to run, often rely on stochastic black-box components, and are applied in exploratory contexts where the expected outcomes are not known. 
Causality-driven testing has recently emerged as a potential solution to these challenges. Building on the concept of metamorphic testing — investigating whether a change to the input configuration yields the expected corresponding change in output — causal testing employs domain knowledge and existing runtime data to efficiently use the limited test runs that can be performed. In this walkthrough, we will use real examples to demonstrate the limitations of traditional unit testing. We will then show how metamorphic testing can go beyond these limitations, how causal reasoning can be employed to increase the efficiency of the testing process, and how the Causal Testing Framework can automate much of this.

title: Geoscience RSE SIG Annual Meeting: Challenges and Opportunities of RSE Careers in Geosciences
abstract:
The geoscience RSE community consists of many RSEs working across a wide range of domains, spanning, among others, climate, weather, space science, geology and oceanography. Yet opportunities to connect across these areas remain limited. This Birds of a Feather session brings together RSEs working in or interested in geoscience to share technical insights, exchange career perspectives and strengthen a growing community.
The Geoscience SIG was formed following a very successful BoF session at RSECon 2024 and following a successful inaugural meeting at last year’s RSECon; this session forms the annual hybrid meeting of the Geoscience RSE Special Interest Group. It will showcase community highlights through short lightning talks and a keynote by Nick Jefferson (University of Leeds) on the development of the African nowcasting mobile phone app FASTA, alongside a panel discussion exploring the varied career pathways available to geoscience RSEs across academia, government institutes, and the private sector.
The session will also provide space for open discussion, allowing participants to identify shared challenges, opportunities for collaboration, and priorities for the SIG’s future activities. We will conclude with an update on SIG activities, upcoming SIG events, and ways for attendees to get involved, such as joining the wider committee.

title: From Fragmented Tools to FAIR Research Infrastructure in Biologics Discovery
abstract:
High-throughput biologics discovery workflows frequently depend on fragmented tools, manual coordination, and disconnected laboratory and computational systems. As scientific programmes scale across multiple research sites, these workflows can become operational bottlenecks that limit reproducibility, traceability, and data reuse.
This talk presents how Research Software Engineers collaborated with scientists to transform antibody cloning and DNA ordering workflows into scalable research infrastructure supporting distributed biologics discovery operations across UK and US sites. By integrating multiple external services through automated API-driven workflows, the platform reduced complex manual processes involving repeated file downloads, uploads, and over 50 user interactions into streamlined workflows requiring fewer than five clicks and no manual file handling.
The system incorporates asynchronous task orchestration using Redis and Celery, Single Sign-On integration, CI/CD pipelines with GitHub Actions, and automated metadata validation to support reliable high-throughput operations.
Beyond operational efficiency, the work demonstrates how RSE practices can improve FAIR data quality and enable AI-ready research workflows through richer metadata capture, improved traceability, and standardised process integration. The talk will discuss lessons learned from embedding software engineering practices into rapidly evolving scientific environments while balancing flexibility, usability, and reproducibility.

title: A Community-Owned Database Mapping dRTP Roles, Skills, and Training
abstract:
As is typical of all digital Research Technical Professionals (dRTPs), Research Software Engineer is a role that encompasses a wide variety of potential competencies and areas of work. Individual RSEs practice a range of skills, often specialising in a particular research domain and/or set of techniques/technologies. 
With increasing professionalisation, a need has grown for this diversity to be documented and mapped. Among other things, a mapping of skills to roles and training provision could facilitate the professional development of individual RSEs, the management of RSE teams, and research into the RSE community at large.
Several recent initiatives have contributed to the mapping of the dRTP skills and training landscape. The community is making unprecedented progress in defining the knowledge, skills, and abilities required for growth in a dRTP career. However, the concurrency of these different initiatives presents a challenge to the community: how can we avoid the simultaneous development of multiple competing standards to describe these things?
This poster introduces a database, developed and maintained by the newly-formed dRTP Landscape Mapping Coordination Group, that describes the roles performed by dRTPs, the skills they need to succeed in those roles, and the training available to equip them with those skills. This builds on the work of many recent initiatives, drawing together previously disparate outputs.
We will describe our collaborative approach to developing the database, explain how community members can interact with it and why they might want to, and discuss our strategy to avoid the “XKCD 927” problem (https://xkcd.com/927/).

title: MetSTAC: Building STAC Catalogs for Machine‑Learning‑Ready Data
abstract:
Machine learning workflows depend on access to large and well described datasets, yet locating these datasets remains a significant barrier to development. Whilst we have the tools required to build these datasets, they are often forgotten or lost, leading to duplicated effort. Within the Met Office, data used for machine learning spans multiple storage systems and formats, making discovery and reuse difficult.
The ML Datasets team has adopted the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) standard as a common metadata layer for machine learning ready meteorological and climate data. This poster presents MetSTAC, a Python library developed to generate STAC catalogs for complex scientific datasets without requiring data duplication or format changes.
We show how MetSTAC supports automated metadata extraction and template driven catalog generation for both gridded NetCDF data and cloud optimised Zarr stores. The poster demonstrates how STAC catalogs provide a single, discoverable view of datasets distributed across local and cloud platforms, enabling users to search and assess data suitability quickly and easily.
By aligning with FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) MetSTAC illustrates the role of research software engineering in building sustainable metadata infrastructure. While developed in a meteorological context, the approaches demonstrated are applicable to other data intensive scientific domains facing similar discovery and reuse challenges.

title: Cloud Cybersecurity for Research Engineers
abstract:
The availability of large datasets and breakthroughs in machine learning have had a profound impact on how modern science is conducted. Once the preserve of computer science, large-scale compute has become a universal requirement across research fields from astrophysics to zoology. This has created a huge demand for computing infrastructure within research institutions, where academics often compete for scarce resources. 
Cloud computing offers a viable alternative. Cloud platforms such as Azure, Google Cloud and AWS offer researchers abundant pay-as-you-go computing resources at competitive prices, without the need to buy hardware or manage software. This flexibility is welcome, but comes with the caveat that operating in the public cloud means working on the open internet without professional IT support. Without appropriate measures, conducting scientific research on the internet exposes researchers and their institutions to security threats that, in the worst-case, could end in sensitive data leaks and ICO fines. 
In this walkthrough, we will showcase best practices for performing research on the public cloud securely, using a motivating example of patient data analysis performed on Azure. We will cover: 
Improving user authentication with 2FA and password protocols.
Protecting your virtual network using a firewall.
Using a remote desktop gateway for accessing virtual machines securely.
Limiting access to protect cloud storage.
Using secrets for managing and sharing sensitive information.
Monitoring cloud resources for threat detection.

title: From Antibody Clones to DNA Order: RSEs Streamlining Biologics Discovery
abstract:
High-throughput biologics discovery workflows often rely on fragmented tools, ad hoc processes, and manual data handling across laboratory and computational systems. As antibody cloning projects scale, these disconnected workflows can introduce bottlenecks, increase the risk of human error, and make reproducibility and traceability difficult to maintain.
This poster presents how Research Software Engineers collaborated with scientists to streamline high-throughput antibody cloning and DNA ordering workflows within a biologics discovery pipeline. The work focused on automating sequence processing, metadata validation, construct tracking, and DNA order generation, reducing manual intervention while improving consistency across experiments.
The project demonstrates how RSE practices can support the research journey by transforming evolving laboratory processes into scalable and maintainable research infrastructure. The poster will showcase the transition from fragmented workflows toward an automated pipeline designed to support reproducibility, auditability, and efficient collaboration between computational and laboratory teams.
Attendees will gain insight into practical approaches for workflow automation in research environments where scientific and software processes intersect, alongside lessons learned from balancing flexibility, usability, and software quality in a rapidly evolving discovery setting.

title: Slurm prioritisation and how to avoid jobs queuing forever while getting more through the system
Automatic Transcription: Building a Safe, On-Premises Service for Sensitive Research Data
abstract:
Automatic transcription has become essential to qualitative research, but mainstream commercial services rely on cloud pipelines unsuitable for recordings covered by institutional information governance. Without sanctioned alternatives, researchers default to consumer tools and universities absorb the risk.
This talk describes how the University of Sheffield moved from a recurring pattern of unresolvable support tickets to delivering Scriber: an open-source, on-premises transcription service that processes sensitive audio and video without data leaving institutional infrastructure.
We follow the full journey: scoping researcher needs; navigating Information Security and Data Protection Office assessments; securing prioritisation in the IT Services delivery plan; prototyping and user-testing with qualitative researchers; writing end-user documentation; integrating with the IT Support Helpdesk so researchers have a recognised route when something goes wrong; and scaling horizontally across virtual machines.
The architectural commitment that made this possible was integrating directly with the existing Research Storage service: researchers deposit files in their usual storage and collect transcripts there. No web application, no separate data store, no data movement outside sanctioned systems. Scriber orchestrates OpenAI Whisper via rootless Docker containers as a background systemd service on a university-managed virtual server. Researchers drop a file into a folder and collect a transcript — no new accounts, no cloud, no specialist knowledge required.
The central argument is that delivering Scriber was an act of institutional translation, not solely software development. It exercises the research-understanding strand of the RSE career path alongside the technical. Scriber is open source; attendees are encouraged to adapt it for their own institutions.

title: Research Software Engineering and Fault-tolerant Quantum Computing
abstract: Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) is a full-stack quantum hardware and software company employing a diversity of skillsets to build quantum computers from the ground up and deploy them into data centres around the world. Quantum computing is often viewed as an esoteric, highly specialised field where a PhD in Quantum Computing is an entry requirement. In this talk we will explore how OQC leverages traditional software engineering skills, including research software engineering, to build the next generation of fault-tolerant quantum computers the world will depend on. I hope to convince you that quantum computing is an accessible field for RSEs and highlight the opportunities which will push the quantum revolution forward.

title: A pitch for sustainable career pathways for digital research technical professionals (dRTPs)
abstract: The growth of the Advanced Research Computing team at the University of Birmingham from ten to over forty members over a period of eight years illustrates the value provided to the University’s research, particularly as research grants have directly funded much of this growth. However, these highly skilled staff have suffered from unclear or time-consuming pathways to advance their careers, through ad-hoc regrading or by applying for new posts at a more senior level. As a result, only 32% of Advanced Research Computing respondents in a recent survey “understand how the university can support their career aspirations,” and this uncertainty leads to costly turnover. As a result, we developed and presented a business case recommending a career framework and promotion pathway to IT Services leadership. In this pitch, we justify our recommendation by outlining how reduced retention of dRTPs compromises the University’s research strategy. We also provide an outline of the finance implications and risks of implementing the scheme and how we plan to mitigate them. While developing the pitch, we identified common themes and risks through discussions with dRTPs across different universities. In this poster, we will describe our business case as a blueprint on how to find common ground between dRTPs’ career aspirations and the University’s priorities and HR and finance concerns. By sharing our ideas, successes, and failures, we hope to share strategies with the community on persuading higher education institutions to make dRTP roles more sustainable, fulfilling, long-term careers.

title: PyEarthTools: Accelerating the use of machine learning for reproducible environmental science
abstract: Machine learning opens up many new opportunities in environmental science, through discovering new insights from data to reduced costs of simulation. However a lot of environmental data does not work “out the box” with standard machine learning tools. As a result researchers need to spend a lot of effort into custom data pipelines for each problem. As the field has matured common usage patterns have emerged. PyEarthTools aims to provide common functionality for the use of ML in environmental science research that enables researchers to quickly build shareable, reproducible ML pipelines for training and inference that can run on many different platforms. A key focus is on enabling common patterns of data access and transformation required for ML. We will demonstrate how a domain specific tool that implements common domain patterns in data and functionality can greatly accelerate research and make it easier to follow FAIR principles. In encapsulating expert knowledge into components and pipelines, this can also make it easier for data scientists and experts from other domains to incorporate environmental science data into their work.

title: Building a Reproducibility Check Service for Computational Research
abstract:
Reproducibility remains a persistent challenge in computational research, despite increasing requirements from journals for authors to share underlying software and data. While such policies are a step forward, they do not guarantee that published results can be independently reproduced.
In this talk, we present the Reproducibility Check initiative, developed by the TU Delft Digital Competence Center (DCC) in collaboration with 4TU.ResearchData repository. The initiative targets TU Delft researchers who deposit the software and data underlying their publications in 4TU.ResearchData. Deposits are screened and authors are invited to participate in a reproducibility check, in which RSEs from the DCC attempt to reproduce the published results using the CODECHECK process (Nüst and Eglen, 2021).
We will share insights from the pilot phase, running since spring 2025, highlighting common challenges and strategies to address them, including approaches to engaging researchers and lowering participation barriers. Based on these experiences, we provide recommendations for institutions and RSE teams interested in implementing similar initiatives.

title: From reinventing the wheel to building bicycles
abstract: There has been a lot of investment in skills and people through a number of DRI initiatives in recent years, across multiple research councils. As a result there have been a number of ovelapping proposals funded either simultaneously or immediately proceeding each other, often with limited visibility of each other. My SSI Fellowship is focusing on identifying what projects have been and are currently funded, and mapping the synergies between them. The aim of which is to share lessons learnt and spark collaboration to move forward together more efficiently than working independently. The poster will be a visual representation of the projects and synergies identified.

title: Porting GLASS to the Python Array API: A Clear View to GPU Portability.
abstract: GLASS is a Python library designed to generate full-universe cosmological simulations for large-scale galaxy surveys. Historically, the use of NumPy has been essential to GLASS’ success, allowing rapid development and integration with a wide range of existing cosmological software. However, as simulation demands grow and high-performance computing shifts towards GPU-heavy architectures, GLASS must evolve to support these workloads. As NumPy was not designed for non-CPU devices, it now poses a significant bottleneck to this evolution. To overcome this, we are porting GLASS to the Python Array API, decoupling the library from NumPy and enabling native GPU execution. By adopting this standard, we are expanding GLASS to support all Array API-compliant libraries, broadening its ecosystem and utility. This transition involves managing varying levels of Array API maturity across libraries and optimising core scientific models for GPU parallelism. The resulting GPU-enabled GLASS provides a significant performance boost whilst remaining performant on CPUs, facilitating seamless integration with GPU-native workflows, and enabling advanced techniques like auto-differentiable simulations via JAX.

title: Accelerating Machine Learning Research in Fusion Through a Pydantic‑Centred Human‑in‑the‑Loop Architecture
abstract:
Training high-performing ML models requires large volumes of high quality, labelled data. While nuclear fusion experiments generate extensive datasets – JET produced 105,929 pulses, each with more than 10GB of raw data [1] – much of this data lacks the annotations necessary for effective ML training. Retrospective annotation is both challenging and time consuming, as domain experts lack the appropriate tools to effectively label historic pulses.
To address this challenge, RSEs and domain experts have collaborated to develop an open-source human-in-the-loop annotation platform for labelling tokamak diagnostic data [2]. This combines a web-based user interface and a REST API built around data models defined using Pydantic [3], with validated annotations stored in a MongoDB [4] database for later reuse. The modular design supports multiple data access layers from different machines, with simple integration of new sources.
Custom ML models can be defined by the user, with training and prediction tasks scheduled via the UI and executed using Ray [5]. These reduce the workload for scientists, who can focus on refining model predictions rather than labelling from scratch. This demonstrates how infrastructure co-developed between RSEs and domain experts, focussed on data validation, extensibility and reusability, plays a key role in the research journey.
[1]: Vega, J., et al. "New developments at JET in diagnostics, real-time control, data acquisition and information retrieval with potential application to ITER." Fusion Engineering and Design 84.12 (2009): 2136-2144. 
[2]: TokTagger. https://github.com/ukaea/toktagger 
[3]: Pydantic. https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic
[4]: The MongoDB Database. https://github.com/mongodb/mongo
[5]: Ray. https://github.com/ray-project/ray

title: From Model to Scenario Engine: A Reproducible ABM for UK Net Zero Analysis
abstract:
Agent-based modelling (ABMs) has increasingly been used to study socio-economic transitions. These computational models feature heterogeneous agents, decision-making, and feedback effects that are difficult to capture in aggregate models. Yet, these features that make ABMs valuable also make them hard to reproduce and evaluate as research software, especially when stochastic behaviour is involved. 
In this talk, we share the software engineering effort to transform a baseline ABM for macroeconomic analysis into a tool for comparing UK Net Zero policy intervention scenarios. The methodology combines design choices, including:
Coding economic shocks targeting different economic markets
A UK-specific data pipeline
Monte Carlo simulation (MC)
Reproducibility controls
Visualisation dashboards
Simulation-based inference (SBI)
We show that a more straightforward separation of the main logic from scenario interventions in the code makes it easier to test, maintain, and extend with new economic behaviours. We also explain scenario uncertainty with MC and SBI. Finally, we discuss how dashboards make outputs easier to inspect and compare for both technical and non-technical audiences.
Although the work is motivated by UK Net Zero policy analysis, the broader contribution is a dialogue of software engineering practices for making large-scale stochastic ABMs more credible and reusable as research software. The talk will be relevant to anyone working on computational models where scientific value depends as much on implementation rigour as on the underlying theory. In addition to making the ABM applicable to policy analysis, we argue that the design choices improve the model's implementation, enabling better software quality assessments.

title: FORGE: tackling four decades of technical debt in an operational forecasting system
abstract:
ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) has been in continuous development since the 1980s. It runs operationally every few hours, drives medium-range forecasts used across Europe, and underpins climate reanalyses and emerging hybrid AI–physics models. It also carries four decades of technical debt, must adapt to GPU-accelerated and external HPC platforms, and is being progressively open-sourced. 
FORGE — Forecast System Regeneration — is a medium-term programme to modernise this codebase: tackling the technical debt, refactoring model and data structures, improving the supporting software stack, and easing deployment beyond ECMWF.
This talk gives an overview of FORGE and uses it as a case study, focusing on two strands of possible interest to the RSE community: (1) a layered testing strategy spanning unit tests, integration tests, and CI on full forecast experiments — with a planned end-to-end clone of the operational suite as the basis for continuous deployment; and (2) the open-sourcing of operational forecasting software, supported by governance improvements: clearer code ownership, review processes, automated linting, and joint development with our Member States.
We share what we've learned so far. Persuading the organisation that technical debt was worth addressing was a significant step. Finding time for debt work amid pressure to deliver new science remains hard, and the debt itself makes things slower. We are experimenting with agentic AI code-generation for behaviour-preserving refactoring as something that might help — using the test harness as the safety net that makes faster, more automated cleanup possible.
A companion talk by Kipling et al. covers FORGE's workflow-orchestration strand.

title: Detecting novel biothreats from global news with AI – from research to production deployment in the Cabinet Office National Situation Centre
abstract:
The National Situation Centre (SitCen), part of Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms (COBR), are responsible for alerting government to potential new biothreats as soon as they emerge. Worldwide news stories are a vital signal for early stage novel disease detection, however the volume of data makes manual review impossible.

In this talk, we will present Biothreat Media Analyser (BMA), a collaboration between STFC Hartree Centre and SitCen which uses frontier embedding models to continuously analyse news stories from around the world, flagging potentially novel biothreats. This collaboration involved RSEs, data scientists, and data engineers from STFC and SitCen. We will discuss the journey of this project from initial ideation and investigation through research and exploration all the way to implementation, iteration, and production deployment.

We will tell the story of this project and the critical role that RSEs played from start to finish. We will cover:
The project journey, from ideation to production.
The ongoing collaborative two-way relationship between the data scientists doing the research and the RSEs turning it into production code.
Architectural decisions necessary to adapt the research from notebooks analysing static data to algorithms running continuously on live data, including the associated trade-offs.
Lessons from delivering research software into a high-impact, high-stakes, information-sensitive government department.
We aim to give attendees concrete patterns for productionising AI research and an understand of what it takes to turn research into operationally trustworthy production infrastructure used in critical decision-making.

title: HPCRSE@RSECon26: 5th annual meeting of the HPC RSE community
abstract:
This event is organised by the HPC RSE Special Interest Group (SIG) to bring together the community of RSEs working in High Performance Computing (HPC) and Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI). The community covers a range of RSE roles from development of research software to support of HPC facilities, providing support to researchers. Our objectives are to provide peer support across the RSE HPC community, share experience and best practice, foster an open, self-sustaining community,  collaborate with other, associated communities and organisations and give the community an opportunity to steer the activities of the SIG.
We aim in our session to be open and inviting to create a forum for network building and provide peer support to HPC RSEs: particularly those new to the HPC area and those working without support from a large RSE group.
The event will be one session, which will be about facilitating discussion amongst the community and will use lightning talk as “seedcorn talks” as the starting topic. These topics will be able to be discussed from a technical, services and training/community view.
To help facilitate the involvement we will use sli.do to enable involvement from both remote and in-person participants.

title: A pragmatic Approach to Technology Selection for RSEs: Lessons from iDiabetes
abstract:
Digital technologies are rapidly reshaping clinical trials, enabling fully remote and data-
intensive studies through web/mobile applications, wearable devices, and integrated health
systems. As a result, clinical trial platforms have become complex software systems, placing
Research Software Engineers (RSEs) at the centre of both development and critical decision-
making around technology selection.
In this talk, I share practical lessons from developing the iDiabetes platform at the University
of Dundee, a digital clinical trial system for diabetes management. I explore how choosing a
technology stack in this context goes beyond identifying the “best” tools and instead
involves navigating real-world constraints such as existing team expertise, institutional
practices, licensing models, cost, and strict healthcare regulations.
Through this case study, I will highlight common challenges including integration of
heterogeneous data sources, sustainability of research software, and the long-term
consequences of early technical decisions without fully understanding the domain specific
context of the project. I will also reflect on the evolving nature of research software as
dynamic, exploratory, and tightly coupled to project lifecycles.
The talk argues that effective technology selection in RSE is a process of informed
compromise rather than optimisation. By sharing these experiences, I aim to provide RSEs
with practical insights for making context-aware, sustainable technology choices in high-
stakes research environments such as digital clinical trials.

title: Reproducibility without compromise: Guix and ravanan
abstract:
We have a reproducibility crisis. Workflows that work on one machine at one time do not work elsewhere or later. Package managers like conda make it easy to install packages on different machines, but cannot help with reproducibility. Docker/Singularity images capture the software environment precisely, but do so by "shrink-wrapping" and leave us with a blob that needs to be stored forever more.

Modern software has accrued incrementally over many decades and has become incredibly complex—a Gordian knot. Programming language-specific package managers (such as pip, cran, Julia's Pkg, etc.) appear to work well but choke up when dealing with multiple programming languages—the unavoidable reality of modern software environments. We need new tools that can straddle programming language boundaries seamlessly and describe workflows precisely.

In this talk, I will introduce Guix and ravanan. Guix is a purely functional package manager that provides strong bit-level reproducibility guarantees and can control the software environment precisely all the way down to the lowest-level system libraries. ravanan is a Common Workflow Language (CWL) implementation that builds on Guix, bringing the same reproducibility guarantees to workflows and providing strong caching. ravanan caches not just on the workflow inputs and parameters but also on the complete software environment. A tiny change deep in the dependency graph invalidates the right cache entries and recomputes just the necessary steps—like a "make" that never needs a "make clean".

title: RSEs as trainers – the who, why and how of providing digital research skills training
abstract:
RSEs often provide training for researchers and dRTPs at their local institution in the digital research skills used in their own work. These courses cover a diverse range of topics, from beginners' language courses, to software architecture and efficiency, to specialised tools and platforms like HPC, AI and domain-specific packages. There are ongoing works to raise awareness of the broad skillset that RSEs and researcher-coders need in order to create good quality, sustainable research software (e.g. DIRECT framework), as well as sharing and evaluating existing training resources.
This BoF aims to gather RSEs who are interested or involved in providing training and to take a step back from the day-to-day rush of delivering content for a wider view. In small group discussions, we will tackle topics such as the process of running a training service that meets the needs of your audience throughout their research journey, the lifecycle of an individual course, and how training is valued and supported at different institutions.
As RSE and dRTP groups grow, opportunities arise to specialise in certain technologies or domains. We will discuss whether providing training is seen as a general duty of all dRTPs, a specialism taken on by a keen few, or a distinct career path. By sharing the attitudes and models of different institutions, we will consider how we can increase recognition of the value that a well-resourced and supported training service can give to researchers and institutions as well as funders and industrial partners.

title: Hands-on with DashVERSE: Building and Customizing Research Software Quality Dashboards
abstract:
As research software scales in complexity, tracking its quality, sustainability, and compliance with best practices is a major challenge for RSEs. The EVERSE project has developed DashVERSE, a customizable dashboard solution designed to monitor and visualize research software quality assessments.
This interactive workshop offers a practical walkthrough of the DashVERSE ecosystem. Participants will gain hands-on experience transforming abstract quality metrics into actionable insights. We will guide attendees through a complete workflow: deploying a local instance of DashVERSE, connecting software repositories to run automated quality assessments, and interpreting the visual widgets populated by the assessment data. Finally, participants will learn to customize preconfigured dashboards and tweak quality indicators to fit their specific domain or institutional needs.
Whether you are an RSE seeking to monitor code health, a maintainer enforcing FAIR principles, or a project lead needing high-level overviews, this workshop will equip you with a powerful open-source tool to promote software excellence within your research community.

title: From research models to a journalist's browser: an RSE story from a 140,000-user verification tool
abstract:
Disinformation and false content produced by generative AI often moves faster than journalists, fact-checkers and human rights defenders can verify. Across a decade of EU-funded projects - InVID (2016–2018), WeVerify (2018–2021), and vera.ai (2022–2025) - research groups have produced a steady stream of natural language processing (NLP) classifiers for persuasion techniques, subjectivity, AI-generated text, and more. Individually, each is a valuable research output. Yet together, they were unusable in a journalist’s daily workflow, being spread across papers, demos, and APIs that couldn’t talk to each other.
The solution is the Verification Assistant, a component of the Verification Plugin published by Agence France-Presse (AFP), which bridges the “research-to-practice” gap. Maintained by RSEs at the University of Sheffield since 2023, it accepts a URL or media file, extracts content, routes it to NLP classifiers contributed by researchers across the project consortia, and returns one cohesive set of credibility indicators. Despite the vera.ai project ending in 2025, the Assistant and plugin remain in active use and continued maintenance. This is a real-world demonstration of research software outlasting the project that funded it.
This talk uses the Assistant as a case study for what RSEs contribute to the research journey on a multi-institutional project. Without RSE input, journalists would not have access to these cutting edge research outputs to fight the spread of disinformation. I’ll cover the technical side (API services, architecture, software surviving handovers between teams) and the coordination side (working with researchers across institutions, the human side of building something collaboratively).

title: Lost in translation? Using the Up Goer Five Challenge to help wonder-driven computer people explain themselves to others.
abstract:
What is a Research Software Engineer? Explaining this to a semi-technical person is already hard. Now try explaining it to a 95-year-old grandfather who was born in a world where computers were people who performed calculations and the closest thing to a modern computer was an abacus.
But the challenge goes beyond grandparents. How do we communicate what the Digital Research Technical Profession is to a secondary school student who has never heard of it? To a postgraduate who doesn't realise it exists as a career path in its own right? To a manager who funds it without fully understanding it? And perhaps most strikingly, to the many people already doing this work every day who have never had the words to describe what they are?
This is the challenge that inspired our submission at Collaborations Workshop 2026. Born out of a hack day pitch that captured the imagination of the room, we built a living glossary that explains the roles and concepts of the Digital Research Technical Profession using the Up Goer Five challenge which restricts you to only the ten hundred most common words in the English language, as inspired by the XKCD comic by Randall Munroe.
Come and hear how wonder-driven computer people are finding the words to make their profession visible, accessible and impossible to miss. Join us, share your thoughts and help shape what it becomes next.

title: Zarr-Cesium: Browser-Native Visualisation of Terabyte-Scale Multidimensional Scientific Data Without Backend Infrastructure
abstract:
Environmental sciences increasingly rely on cloud-hosted terabyte-scale multidimensional datasets stored in formats such as Zarr. While cloud-native storage and computation ecosystems have matured rapidly, visualization workflows often still depend on server-side tile generation, raster preprocessing pipelines, and persistent infrastructure. These approaches duplicate data, increase operational complexity, and separate visual products from their underlying scientific datasets.
This talk presents Zarr-Cesium, an open-source TypeScript library that enables interactive visualization of multidimensional Zarr datasets directly in the browser using CesiumJS and WebGL2. The software streams chunked array data from object storage and renders scalar fields, volumetric slices, and animated vector fields entirely client-side, without backend services or tile-generation pipelines.
The presentation will discuss the software architecture and engineering decisions required to make large-scale browser-native scientific visualization practical. Topics include cloud-native data access, multiscale pyramid selection, CF-compliant metadata interpretation, request cancellation strategies, GPU-based rendering pipelines, and performance optimisation for terabyte-scale datasets.
The talk will also reflect on broader Research Software Engineering themes, including reducing infrastructure barriers for scientific dissemination, designing sustainable open-source geospatial software, and enabling reproducible interactive visualisation workflows.
Zarr-Cesium is currently used operationally within the National Oceanography Centre’s AtlantiS visualisation tool and has been released as open-source software to support wider adoption across environmental and geospatial sciences.

title: UpStacked: A Full-Stack Platform for Inspecting the Evolution of Open-Source Dependencies in Research Software Ecosystems
abstract:
The rapid evolution of open-source software (OSS) dependencies across scientific and software engineering workflows present significant challenges for the maintenance and sustainability of research software. Particularly, RSEs maintaining research software systems must continuously remain aware of updates to OSS dependencies and their downstream implications, as each release could introduce unexpected behavioural changes and security vulnerabilities. However, tools which support the real-time monitoring of OSS updates remain limited, particularly across the diverse range of software engineering frameworks and scientific software tools that RSEs routinely work with. Consequently, RSEs are often required to manually inspect changelogs, which are typically fragmented and accessed through non-intuitive interfaces.
To address this gap, this work presents “UpStacked”, a web application which collates, processes, and visualizes release data from key OSS dependencies to support fast and convenient querying by RSEs. Specifically, the platform’s full-stack architecture ingests and analyses release information for key tools and frameworks across software engineering and bioinformatics. The platform provides change-severity metrics, component-level breakdowns, and LLM summaries to support the rapid inspection of evolving dependencies within research software systems. By improving visibility into OSS dependency evolution, UpStacked aims to support reproducible research software maintenance practices, whilst highlighting the often-invisible software engineering work underpinning modern computational research.

title: Plotting the route from research engineering to policy: a Quarto geospatial analytics toolkit built with and for local government
abstract:
Local authorities hold a wealth of geospatial transport data that has the power to provide critical insights into transport networks in their constituencies. However, this data may not be research-ready or maximised to the full due to constrained resources.
Urban Ride Research is a collaboration between the University of Bristol and the West of England Combined Authority (WECA) to tackle this gap. We developed a Quarto toolkit for transport data analysis, including a dashboard with interactive plotting that draws on both WECA data and open-source demographic data to provide analytical insights. The toolkit is designed to be flexible to meet WECA’s needs: it is written in Python, and Quarto was chosen so that R developers can extend the work in their preferred language. It also supports easy customisation of analysis depending on the policy use case. To support longevity, we are developing training and documentation, so WECA has autonomy over the code and future development.
A central use case has been WECA's Kids Go Free scheme, that delivered over 910,000 free under-16 bus journeys in summer 2025, and which the toolkit allows analysts to interrogate by comparing usage patterns across holiday and term-time periods. Beyond data science, this collaboration has opened channels between local government and researchers, through a data sharing agreement and developing reusable analysis tools.
The talk will explore the role of RSEs in working with local government to understand their needs, ambitions and policy landscape, to provide tools that empower policy makers in data-driven decision making.

title: Making Research Software FAIR with CodeMeta
abstract:
Research software metadata is often fragmented across formats, making it difficult to discover, cite, and reuse software. CodeMeta addresses this challenge by providing a standardized, machine-readable vocabulary (based on JSON-LD and schema.org) that acts as a “metadata exchange layer” across software repositories and tools. 
This interactive workshop introduces participants to CodeMeta and demonstrates how it can improve the FAIRness of the Research Software. Attendees will:

Gain an understanding of the CodeMeta schema and its core concepts

Learn how to automatically generate codemeta.json files from existing software repositories using tools such as Github actions, autocodemeta tool, somef, etc…

Improve your research software metadata by avoiding common pitfalls

Learn a methodology for mapping metadata from other schemas (e.g., package managers, repository metadata) into CodeMeta using structured crosswalks and mappings specifications such as SSSOM 

Discuss approaches to use large language models (LLMs) to generate mappings?
Through hands-on exercises, participants will generate CodeMeta for their own software and experiment with schema mappings. The session targets researchers  and developers interested in improving software metadata quality and integration across infrastructures such as Zenodo and Software Heritage.

title: crawlR: A Large-Scale Analysis of the R Ecosystem Using Static Program Analysis
abstract: Packages play a big part in the development of research software and have a huge influence on the quality, reproducibility, and reusability of code artifacts. For example, good packages can improve the reproducibility of code by providing well-tested, documented, and robust functions. However, packages can also introduce subtle bugs and security vulnerabilities.Over the past months we used flowR, our static program analysis framework for the R programming language, to analyze all versions (roughly 170,000) of all packages available on CRAN. This way, we obtained around 80 GB of raw data on various semantic aspects of the package's functions and variables stemming from almost three decades of R development.We record information such as call graphs, dead code, nondeterminism, usage of R features, constraints on transitive dependencies, compliance with semantic versioning, and much more. Moreover, the data is linked to the release date and download numbers of each package which allows exploring the evolution of these characteristics over time as well as weigh them by the adoption of the respective package and their transitive dependencies.With this poster, we present some of the key results of our analysis, focusing on the consequences for reproducibility and reusability. Additionally, we highlight some of the most interesting and surprising findings, such as the unusually low count of transitive dependencies, the high number of packages that do not lock their transitive dependencies, and the low number of packages that uses semantic versioning correctly.

title: Emerging Practices for AI in Research Software Engineering: A Spectrum from EVERSE RSQKit
abstract:
AI may democratise code-based innovation in ways not seen since the creation of the modern spreadsheet. Research software is part of this new shift.
But tools that broaden automation beyond specialist programmers are evolving quickly, and sensible ways to use them are still emerging. This is especially important in the context of guiding and supporting researchers who code, where the experience of RSEs becomes more important as AI use grows. This is particularly true given security considerations around AI-generated code and the clear need for review and mitigation strategies.
RSEs therefore need a practical model for deciding how to use AI across a spectrum of AI assistance while preserving quality.
Drawing on experience from EVERSE [1] and RSQKit [2], its Research Software Quality Toolkit, this talk presents a spectrum of AI assistance: from direct prompting and tool integration through coding assistants to more agentic approaches.
It examines where these approaches help in practice, including drafting, documentation, testing, support, and routine development work. It also considers how AI use will affect quality, reproducibility, transparency, and appropriate credit, and where judgement, review, and human control remain essential.
The talk closes with practical suggestions for RSEs, projects, infrastructures, and institutions seeking to adopt AI.
The EVERSE project is a multi-organisation EU Funded collaboration, which aims to create a framework for research software and code excellence, collaboratively designed and championed by the research communities.
[1] https://everse.software/
[2] https://everse.software/RSQKit/

title: AppHatchery: From Service Team to Research Partner — Six Years of Building Digital Health Tools and Infrastructure That Last
abstract:
Most digital health tools built for clinical research disappear shortly after the paper is published. The graduate student or contractor who built it has moved on; the grant has ended; the PI has moved to the next project. This is a familiar story for RSEs, we are brought in to rescue software with a codebase nobody owns, documentation that doesn't exist, and a PI who doesn’t understand the lift. Sustainability is rarely planned for at the time the grant is written.
AppHatchery started as a service supporting Emory University's NIH-funded consortium to further clinical and translational science. One RSE, one project. Six years later we are a team of ten with our own product roadmaps, licensing agreements, and brought in when grants are scoped.
What that unlocked was the ability to choose our projects based on the potential impact we can have. The Georgia TB Reference Guide is now in the pocket of every tuberculosis clinician in the state of Georgia; TypeU is given to every newly diagnosed Type 1 diabetes patient at our local pediatric hospital; and Fabla supports over $20M in active research across dozens of studies. These tools exist today because we were financially stable enough to invest in projects worth sustaining.
This talk is an account of that evolution: what the service model costs us, how we failed many times and learned what to move away from, and our current capacity-building model that isn't selling time by the hour to keep the lights on.

title: Lessons from Mapping and evaluating dRTP’s contributions to computing skill and pedagogies in HE
abstract:
In this talk, we will be sharing findings from our research funded by the UKRI’s DisCouRSE Netwok+, aimed at mapping and analysing the provision of digital research competencies (DRC) led by or involving dRTP’s across higher education institutions in the UK.  
The teaching of computational methods has spread across disciplines, spawning numerous pedagogical approaches and a wide variety of methods, software, products, and environments. However, the role of dRTP’s in the proliferation teaching DRC remains unclear. dRTP’s responsibilities are primarily focused on research and infrastructure and expectations around involvement in training and teaching vary widely across the sector. Furthermore, choices as to which approaches and delivery modes to adopt in teaching and training are often driven by trends, licensing constraints or the trainer’s familiarity rather than pedagogical criteria or context suitability. 
Our research therefore seeks to investigate what training and teaching is being delivered by dRTP’s through a detailed survey and a systematic auditing of curricula on DRCs. The findings will be useful to address questions such as: What skills and competencies are being taught? How are dRTPs engaging in their provision? What pedagogical approaches are being taken? What are the main future challenges in the delivery of DRPs? How does this differ across audiences, infrastructures, and institutions? 
We will use this talk to report on our preliminary findings and to further initiate conversations with the dRTP community leading towards evidence‑based recommendations to enhance DRP curricula across HE.

title: Engineering PharosAI: A Federated AI Platform Providing Access to the UK’s Largest Multimodal Biomedical Dataset for Cancer Research
abstract:
Someone in the UK is diagnosed with cancer every two minutes yet the development of potentially life-saving AI models for oncology is hindered by data fragmentation, deficient infrastructure and governance hurdles. This talk explores the technical aspects of PharosAI, a government-funded national initiative between leading universities and NHS Trusts to build a secure platform for multimodal cancer research.
The system harmonises high-quality multimodal biomedical datasets - including genomics, transcriptomics, digital pathology and radiology - across site boundaries via federation. We present a technical overview, explaining how RSEs and infrastructure specialists have led its design and implementation, including:
Software engineering best practice in the development of Navigator: a bespoke portal enabling data exploration, management and automation of information governance workflows, and access to Trusted Research Environments (TREs)
Provisioning of GPU-enabled TREs via infrastructure-as-code
Dynamic presentation of datasets on a per-project basis
Scale-out to public cloud and sovereign compute (AIRR/Dawn) 
Reproducibility via a Common Data Model (CDM) and containerised workflows
Deployment of the Flower federated learning framework across TREs
We focus on the essential role and responsibilities of digital research technical professionals (dRTPs) working at the interface between diverse stakeholders including clinicians, biobanking teams, researchers, data scientists and information governance staff. We also explain how these collaborative efforts are enabling scientific discovery via responsible and reproducible AI model development, while minimising risks to privacy - including navigating the "Five Safes" framework and attaining ISO27001 compliance.

Attendees will ultimately be presented with a blueprint for building secure, high-performance infrastructure to accelerate research utilising AI.

title: Neurodiversity, work structure, and support in Research Software Engineering: an InclusiveRSE and SSI Fellowship survey study
abstract:
Following on from the InclusiveRSE research project "Exploring the Experiences of Marginalised Groups in Research Software Careers", which used an interview-based exploratory approach, this SSI Fellowship project develops a follow-up community survey to support a broader mixed-methods analysis of the experiences of Research Software Engineers (RSEs) with marginalised identities, particularly those who identify as neurodivergent or who have experienced mental health challenges within research software environments.
The project also builds on previous community initiatives within the SSI Fellowship programme, including ConveRSE, developed by Mike Simpson, and earlier RSE mental health survey work conducted by Dave Horsfall.
The project explores how workplace arrangements, including remote and hybrid working patterns that have become more common in post-COVID research environments, may shape experiences of RSE work. In particular, the survey will examine how factors such as work structure, task switching, flexibility, managerial support, and workplace accommodations interact with neurodiversity-related experiences, including those related to executive functioning.
Alongside structured survey questions, there will be open-text responses to qualitatively explore strategies and adaptations that RSEs use to develop sustainable and effective working practices within different workplace environments.
The survey will be shared through RSE community channels, including SocRSE communication networks, and the poster will provide a QR code for attendees who wish to take part or share the survey with relevant networks. By complementing ongoing qualitative work within InclusiveRSE, the project aims to contribute evidence and practical insights that may help inform more inclusive working practices and support structures within Research Software Engineering.

title: Research-ready infrastructure for secure mental health data analyses
abstract:
The importance of Research-Ready infrastructure in the data research pipeline.
Research projects rely on accessibility of data which are also deemed to be of research-ready quality. Researchers themselves do not necessarily have all the skills to be able to implement secure environments to be able to access and analyse data securely. Having a trusted research environment (TRE) designed and constructed by research software engineers/research technical professionals gives researchers access to the data securely, allowing them to focus on their analyses.
The Mental Health Innovation for Research Centre (MRIC) programme was set up with aim to improve mental healthcare by shortening the time it takes to translate research into real benefits for local communities. One of the ways it does this is by providing a secure infrastructure platform which allows researchers to access and analyse mental health data from the Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust securely at the University of Liverpool. This has involved work with numerous technical areas such as data pipelines, data ingestion, landing zones, secure data storage areas, trusted research environments and data cataloguing, to name but a few. The aim of this poster is to showcase how some of these techniques have helped to build this environment and how they enable researchers to be able to conduct their research safely.

title: PEtab SciML: a format specification for solving parameter estimation problems using scientific machine learning in computational biology and beyond
abstract:
Parameter estimation problems are a key component of computational biology studies where systems can be modelled by sets of mechanistic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with unknown and unmeasurable parameters. Scientific machine learning is a methodology where ODE models are augmented with machine learning models, which for example can help with capturing hard-to-describe dynamics. 
PEtab SciML is a data format specification for building and training scientific machine learning problems. The format extends PEtab, a tabular data format for specifying parameter estimation problems, applicable in systems biology and beyond. PEtab SciML enables users to insert machine learning elements into their problem formulation in various ways including,  
To learn dynamic terms in the ODE
Upstream of the ODE, to map high-dimensional inputs (e.g., images) to ODE model parameters
To learn the observable formula, which links model outputs to real observations
To define a Neural ODE, where the whole right-hand side of the ODE system is replaced with a neural network
The format specification enables support for simulating and solving these problems to be developed across multiple programming languages. PEtab SciML problems can be imported into state-of-the-art model-training tools in Python (AMICI) and in Julia (PEtab.jl).  To support a diverse set of ML architectures, PEtab SciML includes a transferrable YAML format for defining machine learning models. This means researchers can use whichever language and ML ecosystem best suits them or their problem, reducing the amount of bespoke code that needs to be implemented to model a new system and thereby improving reproducibility.

title: Ten years of RSECon: what a decade of presentations tells us about the community
abstract:
RSECon 2026 marks a decade since the first edition of the conference. To celebrate the occasion, this poster presents an exploratory analysis of the topics covered across all editions, using the conference's own archive as a lens to reflect on the evolution of the research software engineering community.
To that end, we extracted abstracts and metadata of talks, posters, and workshops from RSECon websites spanning all editions, and classified them by topic through a combination of manual and automatic annotation. The poster presents a brief descriptive overview of some of the metadata, such as number and type of proposals, geographic distribution of presenters, and similar indicators, before focusing on the three thematic categories abstracts were classified into: tooling (those covering tools developed by RSE teams or stack and infrastructure used by RSEs), workflows (those covering ways of working, good practices, and similar topics), and the RSE role and career (those focusing on career development, recognition and credit, community building, and related themes). The poster explores how the balance between these categories has shifted over time, what the community has consistently prioritised across editions, and emergent sub-topics that surface within each category.
With RSECon now in its tenth year, this retrospective offers a data-driven mirror for the community, inviting reflection on how it has grown and what it has chosen to talk about along the way.
(Subject to the programme being published in time, this year's edition may also be added to the analysis).

title: Building multi-user LLM Inference Services for Research
abstract:
Self-hosting LLMs for a research community sits in an awkward gap. It is too "production" for smaller tutorials and academic papers. As a result, almost everything useful about deploying LLMs to multiple users either within a group, a department, or as a shared university service, lives as tribal knowledge. In order to extract this knowledge you need the implementer to have the right mix of HPC, MLOps, and security skills, plus the willingness to write any of it down.
Despite this, self-hosting is becoming common faster than the operational know-how is spreading. Small groups across academia are standing up inference servers on departmental hardware, often without authentication, rate limiting, or any meaningful monitoring. The result is a growing population of unhardened endpoints serving expensive GPUs to the world. This is a real problem, and one the RSE community is well placed to address.
This talk is a practical tour of a multi-user LLM inference service running at Cambridge to serve research workloads. We will walk through the stack, the deployment model, the security layer, and the benchmarking approach used to right-size the service for genuinely mixed traffic.
Importantly, we also address the footguns that don't show up in generic tutorials: health-checks leading to self-bans, LLM containers quietly shutting off, Grafana dashboards lying, and the tension between latency-sensitive and throughput-bound workloads. The aim is for attendees to leave with a blueprint they can adapt including the security and acceptable-use decisions that tend to get deferred until something embarrassing happens.

title: Do All RSE Communities Grow the Same Way?
abstract:
Research Software Engineers (RSEs) play a critical role in enabling modern research, yet recognition, career pathways, and institutional support for RSEs remain uneven globally. While the UK and parts of the USA have established RSE communities and support structures, comparatively little is known about the evolving RSE landscape across other regions, including the highly diverse research environments in Asia, Australia, Africa, and Latin America. 
This poster presents an ongoing community-driven study exploring the Research Software Engineering landscape in Asia through surveys, community engagement, and collaboration with regional and international RSE networks. The work investigates how RSE roles are defined, supported, and recognised across institutions and countries, while also identifying common challenges related to career progression, visibility, training opportunities, and sustainability of research software practices.
The project is being conducted through the RSE Asia Association in collaboration with members of the global RSE community. Preliminary findings highlight the diversity of RSE identities and institutional structures across the region, alongside a growing need for community infrastructure, regional collaboration, and pathways for professional recognition. For regions such as Australia, Africa, and Latin America, we are seeking insights by organising an umbrella RSE conference for the Global South.
By documenting emerging RSE ecosystems outside traditionally established regions, this work contributes evidence towards understanding how global RSE communities can support sustainable, reproducible, and collaborative research practices across diverse contexts.

title: Building a virtual research environment (almost) from scratch for the Heritage Science Data Service
abstract:
Heritage scientists frequently need large-scale datasets and specialist software but often lack the compute and access to it. Many heritage scientists have graphics intensive workflows, and 3D models too large to use on their laptops. RSEs bridge this gap in many fields, and that is why we have built a Virtual Research Environment (VRE) for the Heritage Science Data Service (HSDS).
HSDS is a partnership between the Archaeology Data Service and STFC Hartree Centre, with a consortium of key UK heritage institutions, delivering core digital research services as part of the £80m RICHeS programme. 
Our VRE provides browser-based access to accelerated compute, integrated datasets and software, with ease of access being the core requirement. Unlike a Trusted Research Environment (TRE), we must make it as easy as possible to bring data into and out of the environment. As ever, our challenge has been translating users’ requirements into technical decisions, stitching the right open-source components together while building our own. 
This talk will walk through a few key decisions where user needs have shaped our architecture, from streaming virtual desktops to staging large datasets in and out of object storage. We will show another aspect of an RSE, building bespoke environments where research takes place. Whilst it’s not every day that you build a VRE, we will share some lessons learned that we think are transferable to many RSEs.

title: ePRaSE - an NHS system optimisation tool designed to reduce the levels of patient harms and death attributed to e-prescribing errors
abstract:
According to the Patient Safety Events service, over 700,000 incidents occur annually in the UK, with a significant proportion caused by medication errors that lead to severe harms and death. This talk will focus on how an RSE team worked with a local NHS Trust to build a national tool to help Trusts evaluate the safety of their e-prescribing systems.
Funded by NHS England, the application was developed over a 5-6 year period. During this time, the tool evolved from an initial proof of concept to a widely used application hosted within the secure and restricted Health and Social Care Network (HSCN). The success of the tool has been due to ability of the RSE team to work effectively with NHS project managers, pharmacists, clinicians and IT staff.
Based on significant previous research work done in this area, the tool uses a scoring matrix to determine levels of risk associated with common prescribing errors. Only open for a few months each year, the tool requires clinical users work through simulated patient and prescribing scenarios to reach a final report highlighting problematic areas.
Many of the challenges presented by this project were for the RSE team to understand the clinical domain and data capture requirements; this meant working closely with several highly skilled but non-technical collaborators. In addition, there were various institutional barriers to overcome. Deploying the application within a highly restricted network and changing the technologies used over time also brought considerable levels of technical difficulty.

title: RSE who? A guided walk-through of 10 years of RSE Survey data
abstract:
The Research Software Engineering (RSE) Survey has been collecting insights from the community for the last 10 years. It initially focused on the UK in 2016, then quickly expanded internationally to include respondents from 54 countries in its 2026 edition. This unique longitudinal and global dataset documents how the role, practices, and working environments of Research Software Engineers evolved over the last decade. 
In this walk-through, we will show you the structure of the dataset and guide you through an associated interactive dashboard, which allows users to explore trends, compare regions, and easily extract data relevant to their own question about RSEs around the world. We will also present the community’s views on generative AI in the workplace, based on a new set of questions introduced in this year’s survey.

title: AI tools adoption at the UK's national institute for AI
abstract:
This talk will share The Alan Turing Institute's experience in adopting the latest wave of large language model (LLM) based AI tools across its research and business teams. We will share both the end results - what tools and methods worked well for what use cases - as well as our approach to evaluating these tools and safely and effectively adopting those tools that worked well for us.
Despite being the UK's national institute for data science and AI, the Turing faces many of the same challenges as other organisations in adopting these tools in its day to day work. We'll share the Turing's journey in going from widespread "bottom up" experimentation with LLM-based AI tools to an organisational-level structured approach to exploring, evaluating and enabling the use of these tools across our research and operational teams.
We'll share where, when and how we've found different AI tools effective in enabling and accelerating our work, as well as the approaches we've taken to support safe and effective exploration and evaluation of these tools in a fast moving landscape. Finally, we'll share how we have established a community of practice across our business and research teams, mixing structured support with more grassroots sharing of experiences and good practices to help us all effectively embed these tools in our day to day work.

title: Common challenges faced by RSE groups in the UK, and current solutions to support their contributions to research and career pathways: an interview study
abstract:
One strand within the DisCouRSE Network+ project aims to tackle the systemic barriers to career progression faced by digital Research Technical Professionals (dRTPs) such as RSEs. We are beginning with an in-depth analysis of the diverse structures and promotion processes in use across UK institutions and R&D organisations, on the assumption that different contexts determine the most effective approaches. This talk will present our findings so far and invite others to contribute.
We have conducted over 15 structured interviews with dRTP group leaders so far. Group sizes range from 1 to 70+ people, collectively including 6+ broadly defined professions. Many are centrally located serving their whole organisation, some are embedded within a school/faculty/department, some are distributed. There are a mix of funding models and degree of financial autonomy. Non-staff budgets are available but often squeezed.
Most have more than one career stage represented, with 6 levels being the greatest range. However senior levels usually require managerial responsibility to some extent, and promotion pathways are both rare and often not well suited to dRTPs when they do exist. Most staff are nevertheless on open-ended contracts.
This talk will cover our findings so far in more detail and draw out some “lessons learned” from the challenges that groups have successfully faced, as well as summarising what are seen as key challenges within the sector in the near future. Overall, we see that RTP groups are doing strategically critical work inside organisational structures that were not designed for them.

title: Evolving Research Code into Research Software: A Graph-Based Architecture for CodeEntropy
abstract:
Many scientific software projects begin as research prototypes developed to answer specific scientific questions. As these codes mature and attract users, they must evolve to support maintainability, extensibility, and long-term sustainability.
