This transition is often challenging when the original implementation tightly couples scientific algorithms with implementation details. 
CodeEntropy is an open-source scientific software package used to compute absolute entropies from molecular dynamics simulations, with applications in biomolecular modelling and drug discovery. Originally developed as an academic research code, it has since been adopted and further developed as maintained research software. As the codebase evolved, limitations in the original design made it increasingly difficult to represent relationships between stages of the analysis and to extend the software with new functionality. 
This talk presents a case study of introducing a graph-based architecture to represent the analysis as an explicit dependency structure. Individual analysis steps are modelled as nodes in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), with edges describing data dependencies. Execution order is derived automatically from these dependencies, allowing the computational workflow to more closely reflect the underlying scientific method. This approach improves the clarity of the algorithmic structure and makes it significantly easier to extend the codebase with new analysis methods. 
The talk discusses the motivations for the redesign, key architectural decisions, and the challenges of evolving legacy research software while maintaining scientific correctness and reproducibility. It concludes with practical lessons on aligning software architecture with scientific models and choosing appropriate abstractions for complex scientific workflows.

title: Helping Researchers Find The Way: Optimising the Preparation of Analytical-Ready Geospatial Datasets
abstract: Public Sector organisations have large repositories of geospatial data that researchers have long been unable to take advantage of due to lack of publication in relevant catalogues, being in inappropriate formats, or lacking the computational skills to prepare the data into a research-ready dataset that can be easily analysed. This talk will describe how we have worked with the Scottish Government to create publishable geospatial data products, with the first series of products being the application of an efficient route-finding algorithm to generate routes from each residential address in Scotland to its nearest GP Surgery.  This has resulted in a generic framework that can accept any other “Point of Interest” (POI) that contains coordinates, depending on the researchers’ needs, and we will highlight the diversity of POI data held by the Scottish Government. The resulting data products not only show summary statistics for the whole processed dataset, but the associated metadata allows researchers to determine trends based on one of a number of criteria. We will discuss the computational challenges associated with processing the data, including improving the runtime from 30 hours to 50 minutes on a dedicated high-memory Virtual Machine, allowing us to support researchers with much more agility. Finally, we will describe how these real-world raw datasets have had data cleanliness challenges, and the steps we have taken to mitigate these such that the resulting data products are still of value to researchers.

title: The Fortitude Linter: Don’t Blame your Tools; Build Them
abstract:
Research Software Engineers are prolific users of software development tools: testing libraries, documentation generators, linters, formatters, debuggers, continuous integration workflows, and so on. They’re a powerful force multiplier, and have an outsized impact on the quality of research software in the wider ecosystem.

Fortitude is a new Fortran linter that helps developers to catch bugs early, modernise old code, and keep their code clean and stylish. Starting as an internal tool, it has rapidly become the premier open-source linter for Fortran, featuring around 100 linting rules, robust Fortran parsing, automatic fixes, and IDE integration. It’s also fast – up to two orders of magnitude faster than its closest competitors. With users across six continents, we’ve been able to (indirectly) contribute to a huge number of Fortran projects and make a real dent in technical debt.

This was made possible by piggybacking on the popular Python linter Ruff. Not only was it used as design inspiration, in some cases we were even able to use the code itself to bootstrap our implementation. This propelled us straight to the cutting edge with a fraction of the effort it would have taken to write a linter from scratch. This shows how permissive licensing and code reuse can accelerate our work.

This talk will discuss how research software engineers can achieve greater impact by contributing to tooling. Using the example of the Fortitude linter, we will discuss how we can create or contribute to tools in order to improve software sustainability for everyone.

title: How FAIR is Research Software?
abstract: Research software is a fundamental part of research, and is becoming increasingly prevalent across all fields. Making software artefacts Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) makes it possible to build on others’ research, lowering the barrier of entry for replication and further work by other researchers. In response to this need, the FAIR4RS guidelines define specialised FAIR criteria for research software. However, the current state of compliance in the software engineering research community is uncertain. In this paper, we have conducted a survey on the 246 papers taken from the main research track of the 2025 International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE), spending a total of approximately 124 person-hours checking the criteria against each submitted paper. The results show that 32 (13.6%) papers within ICSE are fully FAIR4RS compliant, with the F criterion being the least adhered to (only 33.3% complied) due to the large number of artefacts being available on GitHub only without a DOI. We also discuss the standards used at ICSE specifically and how they differ from FAIR4RS, particularly relating to the findability and availability of an artefact, which has resulted in the overall low compliance. We also discuss common mistakes made by the submitted artefacts, and what steps can be taken to remediate these.

title: Text Lab: Secure NLP and LLM Workflows for Researchers on HPC
abstract:
Many researchers want to use NLP and large language models, but face a difficult choice: send sensitive data to external services, or struggle with complex local installations, model management, and HPC access. Text Lab offers a third option: a secure, university-hosted NLP and LLM platform that brings advanced text-analysis workflows directly to researchers through an accessible web interface.
Developed at the University of Bern, Text Lab runs on institutional HPC infrastructure and supports local AI workflows including LLM-based chat, transcription, OCR, topic modelling, data visualisation, and knowledge graph extraction. Researchers can analyse interviews, documents, audio files, scanned PDFs, and tabular data while keeping processing within university infrastructure.
This poster presents Text Lab as a research software engineering case study in making complex AI infrastructure usable, reproducible, and sustainable. It highlights the architecture behind the platform, including Open OnDemand, Slurm, containers, GPU resources, shared model storage, and a Streamlit interface. It also shows how the platform supports the research journey, from raw data to insight, while addressing data sovereignty, usability, and reproducibility.
The poster will include example workflows, usage evidence, and lessons learned from deploying Text Lab as a shared research service. It invites discussion on how RSE teams can transform fast-moving AI tools into trusted institutional infrastructure for diverse research communities.

title: The RSE as Translator: Bridging Researchers and Research Infrastructure through DAFNI
abstract:
Research software engineering increasingly involves more than writing code. RSEs are often responsible for translating between domain researchers, infrastructure teams, and usable software systems that support reproducible research.
At DAFNI, my role spans both front-end software engineering and researcher engagement. Working across these areas has highlighted how usability, accessibility, onboarding, and communication directly influence the success and reproducibility of computational research workflows.
This talk reflects on lessons learned from supporting researchers using a national-scale research platform. I will discuss common barriers researchers face when interacting with research infrastructure, including workflow complexity, discoverability, inconsistent user experiences, and challenges in operationalising reproducible software practices. I will also explore how user feedback, support interactions, and iterative interface design can improve both software quality and researcher confidence.
The presentation will argue that modern RSE work increasingly depends on hybrid technical and community-facing roles, and that these contributions should be recognised as core components of the research journey rather than secondary support activities.

title: From Health Economic Models to Decision Support Software: A MedSID/PINCER Researcher RSE Collaboration.
abstract:
The MedSID/PINCER project is developing decision support software to help understand the benefits, harms and costs of prescribing safety interventions. Building on existing health economic models, the project translated Excel based modelling work into reusable research software and an interactive dashboard for decision makers.
This submission showcases two main project outputs: an R package containing tested, reusable model code, and a Shiny dashboard that makes the models easier to explore, communicate and apply. The work involved understanding model assumptions, making implicit spreadsheet logic explicit, comparing software outputs against expected results, structuring the code for reuse, and designing an interface that supports non-technical users.
The project also demonstrates the value of close collaboration between researchers and RSEs. Researchers contributed clinical, medication safety and health economic expertise, model assumptions, expected outputs, stakeholder context and scientific validation. RSEs contributed software architecture, testing, package design, dashboard development, usability, documentation, and planning for sustainable use. In addition, the project explicitly aims to upskill jobbing researchers in robust software engineering practices
By showing both the software outputs and the collaboration behind them, this submission highlights how RSEs contribute to research quality, reproducibility and impact. It also offers a practical example of how RSE contributions can be evidenced through artefacts such as tests, code review, model comparisons, prototypes, documentation and stakeholder feedback.

title: Engineering ASPACE (https://mspace.ac.uk/): Lessons Learned in Research Software Engineering from climate change adaptation research to a decision-support tool
abstract:
ASPACE (Assisted Spatial Prioritisation Addressing Climate Effects) is a web-based decision support tool/platform developed to support climate-smart marine spatial planning through scenario based scientific analysis of ocean climate modelling projections, economic modelling and end-user values, supported by geospatial visualisation. The platform is designed to support the exploration of climate-resilient, socially acceptable and economically viable spatial policy scenarios for nature investors, marine industries, conservation and policy makers, and ocean-based communities involved in marine spatial planning and sustainable ocean management. This presentation will share the lessons learned during the development of ASPACE, covering the journey from requirements gathering through to deployment within a research and decision-support environment.

The presentation will discuss how research software engineering practices were applied throughout the full software development lifecycle, including requirement analysis, solution design, infrastructure preparation, front-end and back-end development, scientific workflow integration, background processing and operational deployment. The platform integrates modern tools and technologies to support marine spatial modelling workflows, interactive data visualisation and output comparison.

The session will also reflect on the practical challenges of balancing scientific requirements, usability, scalability, reproducibility and operational reliability while developing software for multidisciplinary researchers and stakeholders. In addition, the presentation will highlight the importance of collaboration, communication, iterative development and infrastructure planning in delivering sustainable research software solutions.

Through sharing the ASPACE development experience, this talk aims to provide practical insights into how Research Software Engineering supports the transformation of scientific ideas into operational software platforms that enable collaboration, reproducibility and evidence-based decision making.

title: Hiring for diversity and inclusion in digital Research Technology Professional roles
abstract:
The community of research technology professionals are less diverse than those working in academia or in commercial software. A consistent request from surveys is to provide guidance and actionable plans to be able to improve the Equality Diversity Inclusion & Accessibility (EDIA) of recruitment. This session brings together those with lived experience of recruitment barriers, and those involved in hiring to share knowledge and co-create solutions.
This session will be in two halves. The first will be discussion and idea generation with lightning talks. For those who can stay for the second half we will then properly document the discussions, co-working on a guidance document. 
We will start with lightning talks based on real stories of barriers and successes in recruitment, so that we can ground our breakout discussions in practical reality. We'll use an unconference format of proposing and voting for breakout discussion groups in the first half of the session. Those staying on for the second half will produce a guidance document on inclusive hiring practices and produce actions for the SocRSE EDIA and Role Diversity working group over the next year to improve diversity.
Participants will leave the session being able to inform SocRSE’s guidance on hiring, come away with practical steps they can apply to their own team’s recruitment. The guidance document will be openly published by the EDIA and Role Diversity working group, giving the RSE community a shared, iterable resource to raise the standard of inclusive hiring practices.

title: What next for the RSE movement in the UK?
abstract:
Since launching in 2012, the RSE movement has succeeded in many ways. The role has been widely adopted across the research sector, dozens of RSE groups have been founded across the country, RSEs are regularly referenced in UK government policy documents and the UK RSE Association grew into the Society of RSE, a vibrant community with a dozen sibling associations around the world. 
But challenges remain. Professional recognition, evaluation of software as a research output, and institutional approaches to credit are uneven across the country. Generative AI coding assistants have the potential to dramatically change the relationship between RSEs and researchers. Questions around infrastructure, training and sustainability - environmental and technical - have increased in importance in the last decade.
These conversations are happening in pockets of the community but often only among senior leadership or within separate siloes. This session enables anyone in the RSE community to participate in them in a collaborative and open way. What better time than the 10th anniversary of RSECon to identify the issues that matter and consider what might be next for the RSE movement? 
The session will be framed by short talks, offering different speculative futures for the RSE movement that respond to key themes such as training, career progression, and generative AI coding assistants.
Neil Chue Hong - The Craftsperson v. The Scholar
Marion Weinzierl - RSE Apocalypse
Jonathan Cooper - ‘Hub and spoke’ teams
Romain Thomas - Coding is not enough
The rest of the session takes an unconference approach, splitting attendees into small groups to surface and discuss key themes, with support from facilitators to encourage a critical and playful approach.
Collaborative Document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1toc6pAJ_p_Shz9QkL8PjQykp16vcFqb7Zq5S3c5y7YQ/edit?usp=sharing

title: Training the Trainers: Community-Led Bioinformatics Training with Bioconductor Across Africa
abstract:
Community-led training, local instructor development, and open educational resources are increasingly vital for sustaining computational research capacity in under-resourced settings. Through Bioconductor, an open-source research software ecosystem for biological data analysis, training activities across Africa have focused on both introducing researchers to bioinformatics workflows and building local teaching capacity for long-term skills development.
In 2025, Bioconductor delivered three in-person workshops in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Benin, providing hands-on training in R programming, reproducible workflows, and bulk RNA-seq analysis to 83 researchers. Evaluations showed strong skill gains, while French-translated materials and newly Carpentries-certified local instructors improved accessibility and strengthened regional capacity. These instructors, alongside expanded online delivery, will help sustain and scale training beyond the workshops themselves.
Participants across all training sites expressed interest in more advanced topics, including single-cell analysis, metagenomics, CRISPR analysis, and workflow management, pointing to a growing need for specialised training and longer-term engagement with research software and reproducible workflows.
To begin addressing this need, Bioconductor delivered an introductory seminar on its ecosystem to help researchers and RSEs across Africa engage with available tools and infrastructure, and a microbiome analysis series that introduced participants to using Bioconductor tools for research. Building on this, Bioconductor is developing a specialised training roadmap for 2026-2027, including online seminars led by package authors, a pilot advanced workshop co-designed with regional partners focusing on metagenomics in Addis Ababa, and clearer pathways for more advanced training.
These approaches may inform similar capacity-building efforts in other regions where access to advanced bioinformatics training remains limited.

title: TCTrack: Working with researchers to enable FAIR tropical cyclone tracking
abstract:
We will present our experiences working with researchers to produce TCTrack, an open source Python package for determining tropical cyclones tracks. We will discuss how we were able to both apply RSE expertise to improve the software design as well as building deep domain knowledge in the process, ultimately resulting in a better tool for research.
The initial challenge was a fragmented software ecosystem in which different tropical cyclone tracking algorithms produced substantially different results while also differing in software interfaces with varying degrees of documentation (or lack thereof). Researchers needed a unified approach that reduced the barriers to running and comparing multiple approaches.
As RSEs working on the project we identified further software engineering challenges. Rather than reimplementing tracking algorithms directly – which would increase maintenance burden and further fragment the ecosystem – we designed TCTrack to build upon existing tracking codes where possible, with a framework that is easily extensible to enable and encourage integration of other tracking approaches by the community.
Furthermore, most tracking codes produce different, often customised, output formats with minimal metadata, falling far short of FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards. To address this, TCTrack transforms outputs from all algorithms into a common domain-standard format, while preserving metadata from the input files, and storing all parameters for full reproducibility.
Finally, we will present the dashboard provided by the library for interactive exploration of the results. This can visualise and compare the outputs for different tracking algorithms and data sources, and compute summary statistics.

title: Optimising Julia code on GPUs: Case studies from ocean and atmosphere modelling
abstract:
Julia is a just-in-time (JIT) compiled language with a strong focus on scientific computing and performance. It has gained significant popularity in the climate science community, largely due to its flexibility and excellent native support for GPU computing. Over the last year, our team at the Institute for Computing for Climate Science (ICCS) has collaborated closely with the developers of major Julia-based ocean and atmosphere models to optimize their performance on GPU architectures.
This talk presents a series of case studies derived from these collaborations, identifying the specific speed-up opportunities we discovered and exploited. We will dive into the technical details of how Julia compiles and executes code on GPUs, highlighting where performance optimization aligns with traditional patterns in languages like C++ or Fortran, and where the JIT-based Julia ecosystem requires a distinct approach.
We conclude by showcasing the distinct impact of the RSE mindset on research software. By bringing a systematic approach and specialized computing expertise to the collaboration, we are able to spot subtle performance anomalies that lead to transformative speed-ups. This talk illustrates how the RSE's focus on engineering best practices and hardware-specific details directly enhances the capability and scale of modern scientific discovery.

title: The Hubverse: Streamlining Collaborative Infectious Disease Modeling for Public Health Impact
abstract:
Predictive models are an essential tool for public health decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks. Yet the rapid proliferation of models during the COVID-19 pandemic produced a fragmented landscape of inconsistent metrics, conflicting forecasts, and limited comparability, leaving decision-makers struggling to identify reliable, policy-relevant insights.
Collaborative modeling hubs offer a promising solution by coordinating model submissions, promoting transparency, and facilitating ensemble modeling, where aggregated outputs usually outperform individual ones. Hubs also improve communication between modeling teams and stakeholders by aligning outputs with public health priorities.
The hubverse is a modular, open-source software ecosystem designed to support the setup and operation of these hubs. It introduces data standards for probabilistic model output, alongside utilities for hub administration, validation, ensembling, visualization, model evaluation, and public-facing communication. It defines five primary user roles: hub administrators, modelers, analysts, stakeholders, and developers, and supports each with tailored tools.
Built primarily on open-source software (R, Python, JavaScript, Arrow) and freely available platforms like GitHub, the hubverse is accessible even to research groups with limited resources. While hub administration remains the most technical aspect, the ecosystem is designed to reduce barriers across all roles through automation, templating, and interactive interfaces, making it easier for a wider range of users, including public health stakeholders, to engage meaningfully with hub products.
This talk introduces the hubverse through real-world examples, including its adoption by the CDC's FluSight influenza forecasting hub, showing how it standardizes modeling efforts and supports evidence-based public health decision-making.

title: Better Software Funding, Better Research Software? What we’ve learned from the Research Software Maintenance Fund and what you should know about getting funding for software development
abstract:
It can often seem difficult, even for widely used research software, to find resources for its maintenance, refactoring and community development, because the focus of much research funding is on novelty and generation of results. 
The Software Sustainability Institute is running the Research Software Maintenance Fund (RSMF), supported by the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure programme, offering £4.8 million to support and sustain key research software, ensuring it remains reliable and accessible. This initiative is not only funding vital pieces of the research ecosystem but helps us understand what support research software needs to reduce technical debt and grow engagement, and how we can effectively provide it. It is one of a small number of such funds looking to support research software more directly. 
In this short talk, we’ll be giving an overview of the funding landscape, and how it relates to the stage of the lifecycle of your software. We’ll present analysis from two rounds of the RSMF around the types of activities, teams, and areas that are seeking support, along with some of the trends in development practices and use of AI. We’ll discuss some of the challenges of running a fund like this, and how we’ve tried to mitigate them. Finally, we’ll present some reflections on what we’ve seen, that may be useful if you are applying for research software funding in the future and ask you for suggestions about what should happen next.

title: Understanding the community health of research software
abstract: When assessing the community health of an open source research software project, it can be helpful to compare its metrics with those of other projects. This talk will discuss the CHAOSS (https://chaoss.community/) metrics, intended for this purpose, and we will use Augur to analyze the community health of ~3200 software packages that have been peer-reviewed and published by the Journal of Open Source Software, which represent a class of research software: that which is intended to be shared community software and for which the developers seek scholarly credit. We will also compare some of these metrics when applied to JOSS-published software to other classes of software to illustrate key factors that are common for published research software.

title: Finding the thin ice before you fall through: identifying the critical software you rely on
abstract:
Do you know what software you use? Do you know what software you rely on? Do you know what you would do if you couldn’t use it any more?
Research Software Engineers and digital Research Technical Professionals rely on software everyday. That software relies on other software, creating complicated layers of dependencies. But what software is truly critical to your work, either because it can’t be replaced or because the cost of failure is too great? The Software Sustainability Institute has been developing resources and recommendations to help identify the risks to critical software underpinning UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure, along with recommendations for how to reduce and mitigate the risks to research operations.
In this workshop, participants will be provided with materials and guidance to help them identify the software they depend on, how they fit together, and understand how to assess the different risks to their use. They will hear examples of critical software in different fields and the way that risks have been mitigated, before sharing their own examples. They will brainstorm and agree on the risks they find hardest to communicate, and discuss ways of sharing them through different mechanisms.
Participants will leave with both a better individual understanding of the software they rely on, as well as collective strategies to help mitigate risks to its availability.

title: Using nanopublications in research software development
abstract:
Nanopublications are small, structured pieces of knowledge that provide persistent, world-wide accessible identifiers for data sets, events, software, etc. They can be used to capture research information such as hypotheses, claims, negative results, and opinions that would usually go unpublished. Each nanopublication contains three main parts: an “assertion”, the “provenance” of that assertion, and the “publication info” describing the nanopublication itself.

The nanodash project provides several reusable templates to create a nanopublication. This session will introduce the nanopublication template for a research software development plan. Using an openly available research software package as an example, the session will provide a walkthrough of creating and applying nanopublications during the software development process.
The session is aimed at researchers, research software engineers, and developers interested in improving how software knowledge is documented.

title: Marimo: The Antidote to Notebooks
abstract: Joel Grus' infamous, but cordial talk "I don't like notebooks" was eight years ago, but its criticisms of Jupyter are still very relevant. Stale, hidden state can trap novice users, which is a serious problem given that Jupyter is often their first encounter with Python. Since Python is embedded in JSON, tracking changes and dealing with conflicts in version control can be almost impossible. Marimo notebooks address these key complaints. They consist of pure Python, and the execution of cells in consecutive order is  strictly enforced, eliminating stale state. They also allow researchers who have become dependent on notebooks to transition to HPC job-scripts painlessly. Their use of Pyodide and Web Assembly is also better integrated than in Jupyter. Code that uses much of the PyData ecosystem can be seamlessly deployed to GitHub.io sites. This will be demonstrated with the colourful example of a web app for exploring Lyapunov fractals.

title: ConveRSE - Reflections on a year of talking about Mental Health in the Research Software Community
abstract: As a 2025 SSI Fellow, I have spent the last year continuing the conversation around mental health in our community. I've spoken at a dozen institutions and attended workshops on leadership and team culture. In this talk, I will look at some of the common questions people were asking, share some of the tips and advice that I've picked up along the way - both on how we can look after ourselves and on how managers can become better, more supportive leaders. A lot of this will be based on suggestions from the community. I will share my conclusions about how best to focus our efforts, along with some best practices for creating psychological safety and supporting mental health in the workplace, and some of the communities, projects and resources that I've discovered along the way. I will also reflect on the first year of the ConveRSE project, and I hope to have some updates on other projects, training and funding calls that I am currently involved in.

title: Estimating the environmental impact of an HPC job – tools and challenges
abstract:
Researchers and research funders are increasingly interested in understanding the environmental impacts of computational research, including impacts through both energy-intensive computations and the production and disposal of specialised computing hardware. However, these impacts are hard to quantify and often hidden from end-users. While some High Performance Computing (HPC) facilities have implemented custom tools to allow users to estimate the carbon emissions of their work, these tools are not widely adopted.
To understand what tools exist, the methodology they use, and to provide recommendations for tools that are suitable for different computational research contexts, we are carrying out a survey of researchers, RSEs, and HPC operators. We will carry out follow-up engagement with HPC operators to understand the factors that influence their decisions to adopt such tools. We plan to create a catalogue of existing tools, their features, and recommendations for tool developers, in order to promote the adoption of these tools and give HPC users the data needed to better understand the impact of their work.
 
In this poster, we will present preliminary results from the initial survey and tool assessments. We will invite feedback from attendees about their interest in and experiences with these tools, with the aim of starting a discussion about the motivations and barriers to using such tools.

title: Back to the Fortran Future
abstract: How do we sustain sciences currently dependent on Fortran so that they continue to advance knowledge - and contribute to society, the economy and the environment - for the next 70 years? We explore this question in two parts. In the first part, we briefly look at the current state and impact of Fortran-based science and engineering. This includes reporting the results of an international survey of 150 people who work with Fortran code, of which approximately a 1/3 are based in the UK; and describing the range of community development work we have done over the last two years. This should raise awareness and appreciation, within the Fortran RSE community as well as the wider RSE community, of the value of Fortran RSEs. Then, in the second part, we describe our three-year plan to work with the UK and international Fortran-based scientific community, as well as a range of other stakeholders, to strengthen the Fortran RSE community, and to co-design, with a network of interdisciplinary researchers, a roadmap for the future of Fortran-based science and engineering. Whilst this talk focuses on the Fortran RSEs and the Fortan-based scientific community, we believe it has wide relevance to RSEs and RTPs in general, as well as other stakeholders.

title: “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence” – proactively evidencing research software impact
abstract:
As RSEs, at some point we may need to provide evidence that our software actually has some effect on the world. Whether this is for career progression, the REF, just for your own peace of mind, collecting usage data takes many forms but can often come as an afterthought.
In this talk we’ll look at how we can plan to collect some evidence to demonstrate the value of our work and hopefully mitigate some potential future stumbling blocks in our career progression.
Whilst there are a number of useful post hoc forms of evidence such as GitHub stars, package registry or other download statistics – this talk will concentrate on being proactive in our approach to gathering evidence and how, by doing so, the quality and insights gained can be significant.
We’ll go through the pros and cons of different methods for different types of software, think about the different timescales involved and some of the pitfalls and considerations we need to make.
From the highly technical, such as integrating telemetry; to the financial, gathering figures of grant funded research which is supported; or the personal, obtaining testimonial evidence, simply planning ahead can be valuable in the long run.

title: PolarRoute: Optimal maritime routing for the RRS Sir David Attenborough through sea ice
abstract:
Sea ice is a dynamic and demanding environment for maritime navigation; requiring experience and large volumes of fuel. We present work undertaken at the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) to provide a production system on the bridge of the RRS Sir David Attenborough for on-demand calculation of optimal routes through these dynamic environmental systems in the polar oceans with the goal of reducing fuel usage and carbon emissions in the ship’s logistics and scientific roles. 
Building on prior work at BAS to calculate optimal routes using environmental meshes; in the 2024-2026 Antarctic seasons, we built and deployed a production system to provide on-demand route optimisation to the crew. 
This work consisted of several open-source components: 
MeshiPhi and PolarRoute: Python packages developed by the AI Lab at BAS to produce a non-uniform mesh based on sea ice, wind and wave conditions and bathymetry; on which route paths optimised for travel-time or fuel usage can be calculated.
Pipeline to manage the daily acquisition of source data and produce environmental meshes.
System to synchronise daily assets to the ship.
API server to provide on-demand calculation of optimal routes, including asynchronous job management and status handling.
Sea Ice Information System: web client displaying sea ice data on the ship’s bridge, providing a graphical user interface.
This poster will cover the challenges and design choices made to manage the handling of data, models and route requests in this unique operational setting. 
A screen reader friendly version of the poster will be made available online.

title: BioFAIR: Digital Research Infrastructure for Life Sciences in the UK
abstract:
BioFAIR is establishing the UK-wide Digital Research Infrastructure for the life sciences. Funded by a UKRI 5 year pilot programme that began in 2024, BioFAIR aims to address a persistent barrier in life sciences research: reuse of data, tools, and workflows across institutions and disciplines. BioFAIR recognises that adoption of the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles cannot be driven by policy alone: It requires sustained investment in both infrastructure and, crucially, the communities and the people who build and maintain the software that research depends on.
In this talk we will give a strategic overview of BioFAIR, looking at the overall aims and objectives of the programme and our approach to supporting the infrastructure the life sciences research community depends upon. We will outline our “reuse, don’t rebuild” philosophy and provide examples of how services developed by research software engineers are being woven into the fabric of national infrastructure. We will also give an overview of our activities to date, from baselining FAIR maturity across the sector to establishing community-driven infrastructure projects.
Research software engineering sits at the heart of BioFAIR. FAIR data is only as good as the software that produces, processes, and preserves it, and much of BioFAIR's practical impact has come through RSE expertise, in tooling, workflow reproducibility, and infrastructure that outlives individual projects. Looking ahead, the talk will flag emerging opportunities within the programme for RSE-focused funding calls in the coming year, and invite the RSE community to help shape what BioFAIR does next.

title: HPC Carpentry
abstract:
HPC Carpentry aims to develop highly interactive workshop training materials to empower novices to effectively leverage high-performance computing (HPC). This talk provides an overview of the project and its history, explores the content and delivery of HPC Carpentry workshops, and summarises the community's plans for the future. 
Modelled after The Carpentries training programs, the project’s goal is to develop foundational HPC skills, rather than expertise. Workshops provide learners with hands-on experience that elicits confidence working with HPC systems and provides sufficient vocabulary to make subsequent self-study more effective.
In September 2026, HPC Carpentry become the fourth official Carpentries Lesson Program, joining Software, Data, and Library Carpentry. 
The team is currently developing materials for a two day user workshop which introduces the command-line shell  on day one, followed by our Introduction to HPC lesson, covering remote access and resource management on day two. 
Also being developed is a lesson on managing complex HPC workflows using tools like Snakemake.  Future plans include a separate workshop curriculum for developers, engaging with contributors on disparate forks.
A great deal of effort goes into utilising the Workbench, The Carpentries' tool for building lessons. This rendering engine lets us template the lesson files and substitute user-generated values, snippets of code and explanation, or entire custom episode. 
Drawing from the pedagogical success of The Carpentries, we have developed a highly effective hands-on curriculum, leading  novice users across the threshold of connecting to a remote server and invoking the scheduler to properly launch a series of tasks.

title: Does reuse still beat rebuilding in the AI era? (and how can DRIs help decide?)
abstract:
Reuse sits at the heart of both FAIR principles and good research software engineering practice. But generative AI has shifted the calculus. When a working prototype can be scaffolded in an afternoon, does the cost of finding, understanding, trusting and adapting an existing tool still come in below the cost of building a new one? This 90-minute workshop puts that question to the RSE community, and asks what digital research infrastructures (DRIs) should do with the answer.
The first block introduces BioFAIR and its BioCommons, shared infrastructure for data, tools and workflows in UK life sciences, together with the Concierge Services being planned to help researchers and RSEs navigate it. We will set out what the programme is trying to make easier, and where reuse currently breaks down in practice.
The second block is discussion-led. Participants will share how reuse-versus-rebuild decisions actually get made in their own work: what makes existing software findable and credible enough to adopt, what makes rebuilding tempting, and how AI-assisted development is already changing those judgements, including established uses such as code generation and documentation, and emerging ones such as agentic tooling and automated provenance capture.
The final block looks forward. If AI lowers the cost of rebuilding faster than DRIs can lower the cost of reuse, infrastructure must adapt. We will work through what BioFAIR and comparable DRIs should prioritise, metadata, provenance, evaluation, curation, human support, to keep reuse decisions trustworthy, and capture recommendations to take back into the programme.

title: Experiments in Upskilling Researchers
abstract:
It is often part of our job as RSEs to train researchers in computational skills, ultimately improving the quality and robustness of research software. However, delivering training effectively and efficiently to a large group of diverse researchers, with different technical skillsets, interests and research areas is definitely a challenge.
At the National Oceanography Centre (NOC), we (the Software Engineering and Artificial Intelligence team) have been part of an effort to develop and improve digital skills throughout our organisation. Therefore, over the last two years, we have been delivering frequent training in a wide variety of computational skills, largely (though not exclusively) aimed at NOC researchers. 
We have run approximately monthly training workshops and code surgeries, curated self-serve material and are starting to offer very short, one topic training sessions. Much of the workshop materials have been based on Carpentries and Carpentries Incubator lessons, though often adapted to have a more oceanographic or geoscience flavour, alongside some bespoke material. We have run training online, in person and in a hybrid fashion.
Over the course of this time, we have accumulated a lot of experience in creating and adapting training materials and delivering training in a variety of forms. This talk will discuss the lessons learnt from that experience: what has worked well, what has not, what we plan to try next and what isn’t worth repeating.

title: From Theory to Demonstration: A Case Study in Engineering Demonstration Models
abstract:
A recently proposed approach aims to improve the accuracy of simulation results. It does this by combining outputs from multiple lower-accuracy runs, where accuracy is controlled by tuneable parameters such as step sizes or tolerances. This method is called Sparse Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation (SPRE). While conceptually straightforward, implementing and demonstrating SPRE in practice presents a range of non-trivial software engineering challenges.
A key practical challenge lies in designing simulation models that exhibit sufficiently stable and predictable behaviour as parameters vary. In this talk, we share the story of developing such models through a series of visually engaging examples, including animated 3D physics simulations and flocking multi-agent systems, highlighting both unsuccessful and successful attempts. These examples illustrate the difficulty of aligning theoretical assumptions with real computational models.
We also discuss the Python implementation of SPRE designed with performance, flexibility, and reproducibility in mind. A central requirement of the method is automatic differentiation, which we achieve using JAX to compute exact gradients of complex computational functions. JAX also enables just-in-time compilation, delivering significant performance improvements for the repeated evaluations required by the method.
This work demonstrates that implementing advanced methods is only part of the challenge; equally important is constructing meaningful examples that reveal their strengths and limitations. By combining modern tools with careful model design, we show how research software engineering practices, particularly around performance, abstraction, and testing, enable emerging ideas to become usable, reproducible, and compelling software tools.

title: To Pin or Not to Pin: Reproducibility trade-offs in containerised research software
abstract:
Distributing research software via containers is becoming standard practice in many domains for the benefit of improving reproducibility, security, and accessibility to tools that might otherwise be difficult to install or share.
Yet containerised software requires maintenance: package sources disappear, vulnerabilities are flagged and dependencies change. Build once and forget is not a viable strategy for software intended to outlive its initial development.  Reproducible software should be rebuildable.
This talk examines the tensions between reproducibility, security, and accessibility that arise when maintaining container build files. We present practical strategies - from "install latest" approaches to package caches and snapshot services - to keep your builds working. A central argument is that reproducible outcomes, rather than binary reproducibility, is a more attainable and scientifically meaningful goal for most research software contexts.

title: PyActiveStorage: Energy-Efficient Workflows for Exascale Data
abstract:
As climate modeling enters the exascale era, data volumes are outstripping the capacity of traditional networks. The conventional approach of transferring petabytes from remote storage to local compute is increasingly non-viable due to high latency and the unsustainable energy costs of massive data movement. Data-proximate computing, or Active Storage, offers a vital alternative by performing critical analysis tasks at the storage layer. Even when true active storage is not possible, many of the advantages of active storage can be achieved with relatively little effort by the storage system providers.
PyActiveStorage provides a near-production implementation of this technology, specifically engineered for high-performance research environments. The architecture utilizes a modular provider pattern, allowing a unified API to interact with diverse backends. Currently deployed on the JASMIN high-performance object store and optimised for NetCDF4 and HDF5 datasets, the library pushes compute tasks directly to the storage system or an adjacent node.
Using an MPI-style reduction interface, PyActiveStorage executes complex operations in situ. This prescribed implementation allows storage providers to manage security and load balancing while returning significantly smaller data outputs to the user. By bypassing traditional I/O bottlenecks, PyActiveStorage simplifies the transition to near-data processing. We demonstrate how this architecture ensures that as datasets reach the exascale, analysis capabilities and environmental sustainability keep pace.

title: FAIRifying the research journey: equipping RSEs to replace opaque assessments with community-led FAIR definitions
abstract:
While the FAIR Principles are widely endorsed, assessment remains a "black box" of subjective, tool-specific tests that often do not return the same score for the same digital object (https://fairassist.org/tools). For RSEs, this lack of standardisation hinders effective evaluation and use of these tools, which would otherwise be helpful in ensuring FAIR compliance at every stage, from initial planning to preservation, sharing, and reuse.
We introduce an OSTrails framework (https://docs.ostrails.eu/en/latest/architecture/fair-if.html) supporting reusable, transparent, and modifiable FAIR assessments. It will also cover various tools implementing this framework, including: 1) the FAIRassist registry (https://fairassist.org/registry), a Vue3 web-tool for inspecting Dimensions (high-level principles), Metrics (community-specific interpretations of those principles), and Benchmarks (logical groupings of metrics); 2) a FAIR-Test endpoint (https://fair-tests.fairsharing.org), which executes tests from a public FAIRsharing GitHub repository, and 3) a framework-compliant dashboard developed with CESSDA (https://www.cessda.eu).
We will also showcase a new institutional repository FAIR benchmark co-developed by FAIRsharing (https://fairsharing.org) and the Oxford Research Archive (https://ora.ox.ac.uk). Supported by the UKRN (https://www.ukrn.org/fair-institutional-repository-metrics-firm), this benchmark is being reviewed by nine UK and three European universities, reflecting a demand for transparent, institutional-level evaluation.
RSEs will learn how to integrate these "FAIR-by-design" workflows into their own environments, adopting a transparent, reusable method of defining FAIR that is increasingly being incorporated into the UK and European research landscapes.

title: How many RSEs (and related roles) does it take to change a lightbulb in a cage? How RSEs are shaping UK TRE infrastructure
abstract:
RSEs and related roles are critical in building secure platforms that allow researchers to access sensitive data, such as in health and social care. The gold standard for safely providing access to this data are Trusted Research Environments (TREs), also called Secure Data Environments, but most are run by single institutions and often operate in isolation.
This isolation is now hampering research. For example, studies on rare diseases require data from multiple TREs, but current technologies and processes typically do not support this. The TREvolution transformational programme brought together diverse teams of people and roles to examine the barriers to the analysis of data across TREs, and to find and demonstrate solutions.
In TREvolution the term “RSE” encompasses a very wide range of skills and expertise, including software development, managing production cloud infrastructure, understanding statistical tests and limits of anonymisation, creating libraries to support data analysis workflows, developing specifications for metadata, defining APIs and architectures, and integrating with existing IT systems.
In addition there are many more adjacent roles that are often underappreciated and which overlap with RSEs. These include public interest and engagement professionals who bring together members of the public and technical project members, information governance specialists, community managers, project managers, and user interface designers.
We’ll talk about some of these roles, and how they’re contributing to the success of TREvolution. We’ll also look at some of the challenges faced by this large consortium which is bringing together multiple technical projects under a common set of project pillars.

title: Exploring Kiro for Science Productivity
abstract: This workshop will briefly introduce the range of WS AI services and capabilities. Attendees will then be introduced to Kiro, an agentic AI coding and productivity service built on Amazon Bedrock. The workshop will walkthrough setting personal access and introduce core ‘vibe’ and ‘spec’ driven use models as well as core functionality such as model choice and using skills and agents. The workshop is tailored specifically to research use cases.

title: MooBench: A micro-benchmark for performance overhead measurement of observability tools
abstract:
Understanding the runtime behavior of software is inherently difficult due to the unpredictability of the software's behavior itself and the non-determinism of underlying layers, such as Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation in virtual machines, operating system scheduling, and CPU frequency scaling. Observability tools aim to answer questions regarding runtime behavior of software, such as "How much time did this request take?" or "How often did method A call method B?". These questions are answered using telemetry data, i.e., measurement data that is obtained from the code execution. To collect telemetry data, additional code needs to be executed, which introduces overhead. This overhead affects both system performance and the accuracy of the measurements themselves. The MooBench microbenchmark measures this overhead and contains factorial experiments that facilitate breaking down this overhead into its root causes.
The MooBench benchmark was originally developed to examine the performance overhead of the Kieker observability framework in Java and was extended as a general overhead measurement microbenchmark for various observability tools, currently within the Java and Python ecosystem. In this paper, we describe why it is needed, how it is structured, and how it is used in research.

title: Reproducible analytical pipelines for healthcare simulation: Quarto-based guide and dual Python/R implementations
abstract:
Discrete‑event simulation (DES) is a popular technique for modelling healthcare systems, from clinic queues to complex patient pathways. While implementing these models as reproducible analytical pipelines (RAPs) is increasingly recognised as best practice, modellers often struggle to achieve this due to gaps in accessible guidance, skills, and time.
This poster presents a set of open resources designed to make RAP for healthcare simulation concrete and achievable. At the centre is a Quarto book that provides a step‑by‑step guide to building DES models as RAPs, covering project set‑up, model inputs, simulation logic, output analysis, experimentation, verification and validation, style, documentation, and sharing. Each chapter combines narrative with executable code and outputs, and supports both Python and R.
Alongside the book, four worked model repositories provide complete, dual‑language implementations in Python and R. Two simulation case studies, a simple synthetic queueing model and a more complex stroke pathway model, are each implemented in both languages, demonstrating consistent structure and reproducible workflows across ecosystems.
Together, these resources provide practical guidance for healthcare modellers to implement DES models as RAPs, drawing on research software engineering practices to develop robust, testable, and reproducible models.

title: It’s not easy being green: embedding environmental sustainability in training material
abstract:
UKRI is committed to reaching Net Zero by 2040 and RSE/DRI will be key to achieving this. Green software practices will play a crucial role in this transition and so are increasingly discussed in the community - in part thanks to the Green RSE Special Interest Group. For full adoption, we must enable the next generation of RSEs and researchers to embed green software practices in their work through training. In the words of Professor Dave Reay: “Skills are a fundamental enabler of Net Zero” (https://www.theccc.org.uk/publication/skills-and-net-zero-expert-advisory-group/).

Several training courses are now available, some covering high level topics and some focusing on specific topics such as Green HPC and Green AI (see https://socrse.github.io/green-sig/resources.html). The availability of green software courses is of clear benefit to the community and it is valuable to have courses that dig into the details. However, existing courses are not well connected and the green software topic is often considered in isolation, beyond ‘core’ courses such as version control or testing. That is, learners “opt in” to learning about environmentally sustainable software by taking specific green software courses, rather than learning about it in other courses. 
Courses on HPC, testing, and AI are good candidates for embedding small amounts of green software recommendations early, likely also increasing interest in green RSE from the outset. In this workshop, we will discuss how best to embed green software engineering practices in existing training courses.

title: The SHAREing High-Level Performance Assessment Methodology
abstract:
Researchers in many fields are increasingly looking to HPC systems to conduct their research. As the burden on these systems grows, improving the efficiency of researchers’ codes becomes of greater import. However, many researchers and RSEs either don’t have the background and skills to assess code efficiency comprehensively, or may point a single off-the-shelf profiler at their code that does not encompass all domains where efficiency is lacking. This misses major areas where code efficiency and skills could be improved, and in fact researchers may not have the expertise to fully understand and act on the key findings that the profiler surfaces.
We propose a top-down assessment approach, starting with a high-level assessment using black-box metrics split into five categories intended to direct follow-up efforts. Here we lay out those categories and the high-level assessment process.
This poster is part of the SHAREing (Skills Hub for Accelerated Research Environments Inspiring the Next Generation) project. Part of this project is to create a performance assessment and analysis methodology, with the intention that researchers will be able to more easily perform comprehensive high-level performance assessment and use appropriate tooling to improve their code.

title: Social Infrastructure: The Human Work Behind Open Scientific Computing
abstract:
Open, interactive computing infrastructure depends on more than good code. It depends on connection, understanding, and moving ideas into action: the “soft” skills that are often treated as secondary to technical work but are in fact foundational to it.
Drawing on experience building 2i2c’s community-driven model for shared research computing infrastructure, and on stories from people across the Jupyter and open scientific Python communities, this talk makes the case that connection-building work is not a nice-to-have alongside technical infrastructure;  it is infrastructure. Through five practices, grounded in open source community members’ work, we’ll explore how small actions turn big visions into reality.
Attendees will leave with concrete practices they can bring back to their own research software communities, and a stronger case for why “soft skills” deserve a seat at the table in technical infrastructure work.

title: We’ve Built a Great RSE Community. Now Let’s Try to Save the Planet.
abstract:
Digital research is vital to society; it underpins discoveries from new cancer treatments to climate modelling. But digital research also has an environmental impact that's largely invisible to the users. 
Research institutions and funders are increasingly setting environmental policies which aim to reduce the environmental impact of research, but it is not always clear how this affects the day-to-day work of researchers and RSEs.  What should RSEs do to respond to these policies?

This talk explores the role research software engineers can play in turning environmental targets into practice, and the skills needed to do it. It will explore the power that we all hold to advocate for change so that we can help create a change that benefits both the planet and our community.

title: Speed vs Structure: Building Reproducible AI Workflows with the UCL Unified AI Research Platform
abstract:
In this 30-minute walk-through, we demonstrate how AI model development can be effectively balanced between rapid experimentation and robust, reproducible software engineering practices using Unified AI, UCL’s in-house Kubernetes-based research platform. 
Through an end-to-end example using open-access datasets to train a foundational model for synthetic image generation (https://github.com/xfetus/fetal-ultrasound-edm2), we present two complementary workflows. First, we demonstrate rapid prototyping using Kubeflow-TrainerCommand with the notebook training-edm2-model-scratch-volume.ipynb, where dependencies are installed and training is executed directly in a scratch volume. This enables fast iteration and exploratory development, allowing researchers to quickly validate ideas and test modelling assumptions with minimal setup. We then move to a structured, production-oriented workflow using training-edm2-model-ghcr.ipynb. Here, containerised environments and a central GitHub image registry manage code and dependencies, with execution still handled via Kubeflow-TrainerCommand. This highlights how the same task can support reproducibility, version control, scalability, and long-term maintainability. 
We highlight trade-offs between speed and robustness in real-world AI workflows. The session is reproducible for UCL researchers with Unified AI accounts and useful for external participants exploring practical adoption. It is designed to encourage discussion before and after the event, support knowledge exchange, and foster future collaboration. 
We conclude by reflecting on broader good practice, including how institutional platforms such as Unified AI, currently an in-house UCL platform requiring UCL ID credentials, can reduce reliance on external vendors, improve cost efficiency, and support more consistent and reproducible research across teams. This also creates opportunities for cross-faculty collaboration and discussion of how similar approaches are being adopted elsewhere.

title: Code Translation using Large Language Models: What's the role of the Research Software Engineer?
abstract:
Translating research code to other programming language enables researchers to reach beyond their own domain, increasing research impact whilst guarding against software obsolescence. Successful translation requires skills in both the source and target language, and the research domain; it is unlikely that any individual will be able to perform translation. Large language models (LLMs) support translation by amalgamating language and domain knowledge from many sources. RSEs play a role in this by implementing best practice and providing validation tools.

We will discuss our experiences in developing a Claude Code plugin to support domain experts in statistics in translating Stata packages to R and Python.  
The plugin implements 4 skills;
1. Analyse and plan: Is the package well documented and tested? Which target language(s)? Create a new library or contribute to an existing library?
2. Translation to pseudocode: Translation to pseudocode supports human review without language expertise. Excludes any existing tests.  
3. Pseudocode to target language(s): Translate; add infrastructure to support ongoing opensource development (CI testing, contributing guidelines, licenses).  
4. Tests and documentation: Implement any existing Stata tests in target language; summarise test correspondence; highlight missing tests. Review documentation (examples, papers), and translate to target language (eg. Vignettes in R)  
 
We used the plugin in workshops with statisticians to translate a selection of Stata packages. We will discuss our experiences from the workshops and compare our results with existing research in code translation. We aim to provoke informed discussion about the role of RSEs and LLMs in code translation.

title: How-to: Regional RSE Groups
abstract:
In this 90-minute interactive speed-writing session, we will co-author a guide for: creating and sustaining a regional RSE group, engaging with the regional community and hosting a regional RSE event. We aim to bring together a wealth of siloed knowledge from across different regional RSE communities for the benefit of everyone. We are interested in hearing from a diverse group of people who would like to support regional RSE communities. All are welcome, whether or not you are a member of an existing regional RSE group, or are a current or aspiring organiser of a regional RSE group.
During the event you will directly contribute to structured HackMD templates for several pre-identified themes. You will divide into breakout groups and organisers, selected from key figures within the regional RSE community, will act as guides, scribe and hybrid facilitator for each group.
Participants in this workshop will be co-authors of all the discussion materials (made available under a CC-BY licence) including a blog post on the SocRSE website (https://society-rse.org/announcements/) and longer-form guidance and resources on the Regional Groups page (https://society-rse.org/community/regional-groups/) which will be curated by organisers and volunteers after the event.

title: The Journal of Open Source Software - An Introduction and Recent Changes
abstract:
The Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS; https://joss.theoj.org) publishes concise peer-reviewed articles describing open source research software. The review process is open, iterative and includes evaluation of the software and its related attributes. The primary objectives are to promote software and those who develop it as a key part of the research process, whilst also encouraging good software practices in research. For RSEs JOSS presents an avenue through which they can be recognised for their contributions to research in formal literature.
This poster aims to improve community awareness of JOSS for research software projects and encourage submission from the RSE community. For those already aware of JOSS we encourage engagement with the journal not only as authors, but also as part of the volunteer community of reviewers and editors.
In the past year JOSS experienced a change in scope in response to the changing landscape in relation to AI-generated code. Part of the poster will raise awareness of these changes by communicating them to the RSE audience. We will discuss the reasons for these alongside related submission data.
Finally, RSECon26 is running a partnership with JOSS through which authors can submit their work to the journal and also present it at the conference as part of a special issue. We hope to highlight and celebrate this collaboration.

title: From Bottleneck to Breakthrough: A Hands-On Workflow for Profiling and Optimizing HPC Applications on AMD GPUs
abstract:
Modern HPC applications can leave significant performance on the table, but identifying the real bottleneck is often harder than writing the code. This hands-on tutorial teaches attendees a practical, profiling-driven workflow for understanding, diagnosing, and improving GPU application performance on AMD Instinct™ GPUs.

Using a 2D shallow-water solver as a running example, participants will follow the complete optimization journey from initial measurement to multi-node scaling. Along the way, they will learn how to select the right profiling tool for the question they are trying to answer, interpret performance data with confidence, and turn profiler output into actionable optimization decisions.

In Part 1, attendees will build a foundation in performance analysis by exploring the ROCm profiling ecosystem and learning how different tools reveal application behavior at the kernel, system, and instruction levels. In Part 2, they will apply those techniques to improve single-GPU performance, using profiling evidence to uncover hardware underutilization, synchronization overheads, and inefficient execution patterns. In Part 3, they will extend the same workflow to MPI-based multi-process applications, diagnosing communication bottlenecks, analyzing scaling behavior, and implementing optimizations that improve parallel efficiency.

By the end of the session, attendees will have a repeatable methodology for profiling and optimizing scientific applications, a stronger understanding of GPU performance analysis concepts such as roofline modeling and timeline analysis, and practical experience applying these techniques on AMD hardware. All example code and profiling recipes will be open source, and attendees will have access to AMD MI300A APUs during the tutorial.

title: Accelerating research by leveraging AWS: AIRR Cloud Pilot and SENSE
abstract:
Frontier research has increased compute requirements with the rise of massive datasets and LLMs. The Hartree Centre has leveraged AWS resources to meet accelerating demand, ensuring the UK can stay at the cutting edge. The flexibility, performance and reliability of AWS have been key drivers of successful projects across the UK business and research community. 
The AI Research Resource (AIRR), a UKRI/BIST programme that provides AI-specialised compute capacity to researchers, academia and industry, is expanding its offering to include the cloud. In the AIRR Cloud Pilot we have enabled rapid access to the public cloud for UK research and industry. Cloud offers access to dedicated frontier GPUs and compute, managed AI services such as AWS Bedrock and the ability to scale quickly from prototype to production. Beyond the flexibility in compute offerings, cloud access is helping users close the gap between research and production. 
The Smart Energy Data Service (SENSE) is a hub for large energy datasets. As a public facing service with hybrid data, it was critical to have a highly reliable and scalable storage solution. The platform combines a data lake and warehouse on AWS, taking advantage of cost-effective object storage to scale to massive datasets. A distributed service design ensures the SENSE platform is resilient and expandable with new features. 
This talk will showcase how AIRR Cloud Pilot and SENSE leverages flexible cloud infrastructure to give researchers access to the compute and data they need to accelerate the journey from experimentation to real world impact.

title: Introduction to AIRR
abstract:
This workshop offers a practical introduction to the AI Research Resource (AIRR) for Research Technical Professionals, covering the access process and the AIRR systems. 
We begin with an overview of AIRR access calls and AIRRPortal, equipping attendees with the knowledge needed to apply for and manage compute allocations. 
The Bristol Centre for Supercomputing will introduce Isambard-AI, structured around the practical workflow a new user follows: connecting to the system via Clifton and SSH, installing and managing software including ML frameworks, and submitting and managing jobs with Slurm. Each section combines a short presentation on the design decisions behind the relevant part of the system and follows with a demonstration, giving attendees both the conceptual grounding and the practical experience to work confidently on Isambard-AI. 
Following this, the University of Cambridge will introduce the Zenith Supercomputer, and the Zenith LLM Inference Service. We give a brief overview of how the service works, and how to connect, followed by a practical session for users, showing a few use cases and applications.

title: Imago - making satellite data useful, usable and used
abstract:
Satellite observations provide unparalleled insight into spatio-temporal processes on our planet, and are extensively used by many communities. However, their use in the social sciences and policymaking has historically been limited by technical, computational, and methodological barriers. Imago, a consortium of research software engineers, data scientists and social/policy experts addresses this gap, transforming terabytes of complex Earth Observation data into digestible, actionable insights for social scientists and policymakers. RSEs are embedded throughout the project, shaping not only the design of the software and technical infrastructure but also the underlying scientific questions.
Imago comprises several data products, which focus on key knowledge gaps in these communities. We are developing an extensive library of training and workshops to upskill non-experts in how best to use and interpret our data, ensuring that our outputs are usable and reusable beyond the project itself. Central to Imago is the ongoing development of imago, an open-source Python library designed to streamline processing workflows; parallelising and optimising the process of obtaining satellite data and the key processing steps needed to transform raw pixels into actionable insights.
We demonstrate this approach through the Sun Probability Framework (SPF), a novel data product that converts underutilised satellite cloud mask data into meaningful measures of sunlight exposure. SPF combines scalable, parallel processing via the imago library with new algorithms designed to quantify and correct systematic biases. The result is a rigorously validated, reproducible software pipeline, the results of which are ready for immediate use in social research.

title: Following Scrum with part-time teams: Experiences of delivering high-quality Git and GitHub documentation for Met Office employees, partners and collaborators
abstract:
The Met Office has relied on Subversion and Trac for research software version control and project management for over 20 years. In June 2023, the Science Git Migration Project was launched to support the widespread and business-critical transition to Git and GitHub. 
To support Science Git Migration Project activities, a community of Git and GitHub Champions was formed to utilise and consolidate expertise from across the organisation. These Champions enthusiastically volunteer their time alongside their day jobs to: 
Champion the use of Git and GitHub.
Share knowledge, skills, and good practice.
Work collaboratively.
Provide help and support to colleagues.
One of the activity teams supported by the Git and GitHub Champions is the documentation team. This team develops documentation containing Met Office context, enabling Met Office employees, partners and collaborators to effectively find reliable information, advice, and good practice. This supports them to use Git and GitHub in a competent, efficient, and productive way. 
The documentation team follows the Scrum framework to deliver high-quality content. However, as all contributors work part-time on a voluntary basis, the team does not engage in every Scrum Event or Commitment. Over nearly a year of collaboration, including a two-month period with full-time contributors, we explored how different levels of availability affected communication, planning and reviewing, and how to maintain sustainable progress without dedicated project time. 
This talk discusses the different approaches we trialled to balance quality, momentum, and contributor wellbeing, and shares lessons learned about delivering high-quality content through a volunteer, part-time community.

title: Training to Protect Research Integrity in the Age of AI-assisted Coding
abstract:
The use of generative AI tools to generate source code or to augment a programmer's own code is ever more widespread in research software development. While evidence of associated gains in productivity is far from settled, little doubt remains that large language models are capable of generating relatively extensive volumes of runnable source code. The availability of this technology has deep implications for research, including for the development and maintenance of Research Software. As adoption grows, a proactive, multi-faceted response is required from the RSE community to ensure the integrity of research, including through updated training programmes.
This talk will summarise the approach being taken by the AI Carpentry project, to build a Community of Practice around the development and delivery of training and education in research computing skills including Research Software Engineering. 
We will give an overview of the curriculum we have created to help researchers and RSEs make informed decisions about whether and how to use LLMs in the development of research software, and reflect on recent experiences from teaching these lessons in workshops. We will discuss some of the challenges associated with developing training in a rapidly changing technological landscape, and AI Carpentry’s plans to tackle them. And we will explore the tension between teaching the use of large language models and remaining aligned with the core values of The Carpentries.

title: Reflecting on things that didn’t go to plan
abstract: We often conflate things not going to plan with things going wrong. In this talk, I'll challenge this idea by talking about a period of my life which didn't go to plan and reflecting on whether things really did go wrong as a consequence. I'll share what I learned and hopefully how those learnings apply not just in general life, but also in our work as RSEs.

title: From Code to Civic Power: Rethinking Research Software as Public Infrastructure
abstract: This talk explores what happens when research software principles are applied to civic systems. Drawing from the experience of building OpenGov Africa, it looks at how software can structure informal data, support citizen participation, and make governance more transparent and collaborative. It offers a perspective from environments where infrastructure is still being built, and where software has the potential to shape not just research, but public life itself.

title: Cloud-Native SIG Workshop: Deploying a Web Application with Kubernetes
abstract:
The academic world is asking for more web-based software to make research more accessible to both researchers and the public. There are many challenges with writing, maintaining and deploying web services, so how, as an RSE can we make this journey easier. Cloud-Native technology (Kubernetes) is a very easy and stable way for researchers to deploy cloud-based web applications and can be run on everything from a local laptop, Raspberry Pi or HPC reducing the need for a public cloud provider to run your web apps.  This workshop is designed for new starters to Kubernetes who wish to have a practical demonstration of how this technology works. We will provide a hands-on tutorial of how:
To deploy a simple web application on Minikube
To make updates to your website
Kubernetes can automatically recover when there are underlying problems.
Last year this workshop was very popular, so building on feedback and other refinements we are redelivering it to RSEs of all career stages who are interested in web applications, DevOps or deployment.

title: DIRECT: How a community idea evolved into a thriving Digital Research Competencies Framework
