abstract:
Research software engineers and other digital research technical professionals (dRTPs) play a critical role throughout the research lifecycle, yet the skills required for these roles remain difficult to define, recognise and develop. Existing competency frameworks often fail to capture the unique blend of technical, domain, collaborative and interpersonal expertise required in research environments.
The Digital Research Competencies (DIRECT) Framework addresses this gap through a community-driven approach to defining and structuring the skills needed for modern digital research. Emerging from grassroots discussions at the Software Sustainability Institute Collaborations Workshop in 2023, DIRECT has evolved through sustained engagement with the RSE community and beyond, incorporating perspectives from domains including green computing, high-performance computing and digital humanities.
It is also situated within the broader UKRI-funded DisCouRSE Network+ and the national dRTP landscape coordination effort, which aim to strengthen leadership, career pathways, and cross-community alignment for dRTPs.
We present the evolution of DIRECT from an initial idea to a growing ecosystem comprising a competency framework, community practices, and an interactive web-based tool. Key insights from this process include the importance of community ownership, challenges in defining transferable competencies across diverse roles, and lessons learned from engaging diverse research domains.
We demonstrate how DIRECT can be used in practice to support career development, identify team skills gaps, and help institutions better recognise and plan for digital research expertise. We show how competency frameworks can strengthen the role of RSEs across the research lifecycle while improving recognition, quality, and reproducibility of research software.

title: A Community Led Risk Register for Responsible AI in Research Software Engineering
abstract:
Adoption of AI tools into research software practices is becoming an increasingly common part of modern RSE practice, yet the community lacks a shared framework for understanding and responding to the risks it introduces. As such, individual practitioners are too often left to navigate the unintended consequences of AI adoption alone, and leaders, institutions and policy makers lack clear visibility of the concerns emerging from RSE practice.
Building on an earlier event at Collaborations Workshop 2026, this Birds of a Feather session introduces the Responsible AI Risk Register for Research Software Engineering (RAIRR): a living, community-supported resource that documents risks RSEs have encountered during AI adoption, alongside mitigations, examples of best practice, and assessments of risks’ likelihood, severity, and reach. The register is openly hosted on GitHub and designed for continuous contribution from the RSE community.
Working in small groups, participants will discuss the risks most relevant to their own practice, submit new contributions directly to the live register, and comment on other groups' submissions. By the end of the session, attendees will have experienced the full contribution lifecycle and made a meaningful, lasting addition to a  public community resource.
The session is led by the Software Sustainability Institute's Responsible AI in RSE study group, and serves as an open invitation to join. No prior knowledge is needed - if you use AI tools in your RSE work, or are simply curious about how the community is thinking about responsible adoption, this session is for you.

title: Evolving the RSE role in the age of generative and agentic AI
abstract:
Generative AI and agentic tools (GenAI) are dramatically changing research software practice. Researchers can now generate their research code more easily with less programming and software engineering experience. Anecdotal evidence suggests that researchers’ collaborations with RSEs now focus on more complex or higher-level software engineering tasks such as code review.

These changes bring uncertainty: Will the RSE role be reduced to reviewing and refactoring AI-generated codebases, or combining prompt engineering and configuring agentic workflows? How can we assert the value of RSEs to our institutions, funders, and collaborators in the future? Will agentic systems replace RSEs and RSE groups?

We present a vision for the future of the RSE role and its value proposition, developed at a recent ReSA workshop (https://www.researchsoft.org/events/rse-ai-workshop/). We believe that while the RSE role will change with GenAI, its value remains because of RSEs’ unique insight into the interplay between research methods and software engineering. RSEs combine deep understanding of research disciplines with professional software engineering expertise, which is critical to the collaborative effort of research in assuring that sustainable research software supports the highest quality reproducible research. To realise this value, the RSE role will increasingly integrate expertise in relevant GenAI methods and tools.

We summarise our discussion and propose a roadmap for future collaboration within the research software community to develop measures for future-proofing research software engineering and the RSE role. We also highlight early outcomes from a Birds-of-a-Feather session on this topic, held at the 1st International Research Software Conference.

title: PRO4RS - Developing, aligning, and implementing policies on research software for research performing organisations
abstract: Research software is essential to modern science, yet many research-performing organisations lack coherent policies to support its development, sustainability, and recognition. Despite its central role in research outcomes, research software and its personnel are often excluded from research institution policies. This talk discusses the work of the Policies in Research Organisations for Research Software (PRO4RS) Working Group, exploring current gaps, including limited support for research software personnel, and offering recommendations for embedding software into policy frameworks to ensure the software is valued, sustained, and aligned with broader research goals. The analysis proposes a three-layer framework to guide policy development: central policies that explicitly recognise software as a scholarly output; middle-layer policies that align related areas such as open science, intellectual property, and research evaluation; and outer-layer mechanisms like guidelines and frameworks that enable practical implementation. Institutions are encouraged to assess existing practices, adopt international declarations, and engage stakeholders to advance software recognition. Stronger institutional policies can foster good practices, boost collaboration, support reproducibility, and strengthen researcher development, to maximise both institutional value and research impact, and position organisations as leaders in open, sustainable, software-driven science.
